_note: One story per concept, written at three reading levels. 2nd grade is pinned to what its own lesson has taught, because the youngest readers are the ones a decodable text is really for. 3rd and 4th are given a floor of all Level 3 and all Level 4, since the levels track the grades. Each level carries three comprehension questions with answers and a writing task of a type that grade is expected to write. Checked by scripts/check-passages.mjs. Written for Upshift, not copied from any published reader.

g2.title: Nat and the Map
paras: Nat is a cat. Nat has a tan hat. The hat is not big. It is a cat hat.
Dad sat on a mat. Dad had a map. The map was for a run up to see Nan.
Nat ran at the map. Nat sat on it. “Get up, Nat,” said Dad. Nat did not get up.
Dad put the map on his lap. Nat sat on the lap. Nat had a nap on Dad.
Dad can see the map now. Nat can nap. Dad and Nat are pals.
qs: What does Nat sit on at the start?
Nat sits on the map.
Why does Dad put the map on his lap?
So he can see the map and Nat can still sit on him.
How do you know Nat and Dad are pals?
Nat naps on Dad and Dad lets him stay.

write.task: Tell what Nat did, in order. Use first, next, and last. End by telling how Dad felt.

g3.title: Nat and the Map
paras: Nat is a tan cat with one black ear. He has a hat that Dad made from an old bag, and he wears it all day long.
On Saturday, Dad sat on the mat with a big paper map. He was planning a trip to see Gram in the next town.
Nat ran straight at the map and sat down right on top of it. “Get up, Nat,” said Dad. Nat did not move one bit.
Dad thought for a moment. Then he lifted the map onto his lap. Nat climbed up after it and curled into a ball.
Now Dad could read the map, and Nat could nap. They both got what they wanted, which is how it usually goes with pals.
qs: Where was Dad planning to go?
To the next town to see Gram.
What problem did Nat cause?
He sat in the middle of the map so Dad could not read it.
How did Dad solve the problem without moving Nat?
He lifted the map onto his lap so Nat could sit there too.

write.task: Rewrite this story as Nat the cat telling it. Use time-order words and at least one line of dialogue.

g4.title: Nat and the Map
paras: Nat is a tan cat with a single black ear and a strong opinion about where he belongs, which is always directly on top of whatever a person is trying to use.
On Saturday morning, Dad spread a paper map across the mat and began tracing the road to Gram's town with one finger. Nat watched from the doorway, tail twitching.
He crossed the room in four quick steps and settled himself in the exact centre of the map, folding his paws under his chest as if he had been invited.
“Get up, Nat,” Dad said. Nat closed his eyes. Dad tried lifting one corner, then the other. The cat stayed put, heavy and completely unbothered.

In the end Dad gave up arguing and lifted the whole map onto his lap. Nat climbed aboard, turned twice, and fell asleep. Dad read the route over a warm, rumbling cat, which is the sort of compromise you learn to make with a pal.
qs: What does the first paragraph tell you about Nat's character?
He always sits on whatever a person is trying to use.
Why does the author say Nat sat 'as if he had been invited'?
To show Nat thinks he has every right to be there.
What does Dad's choice at the end show about him?
He would rather compromise than argue with the cat.

write.task: Was Dad right to give in to Nat? State your opinion, support it with two reasons and details from the story, and finish with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Pig in the Pen
paras: Rob has a pig. The pig is big. Rob put the pig in a pen.
The pig did not sit. He dug in the mud. He dug a pit by the log.
Then the pig was out. He ran in the sun. He sat in the wet mud and did not get up.
Rob ran to get him. The pig ran too. Rob sat down in the mud.
Now Rob is wet. The pig is wet. Rob did not get mad. He let the pig sit in the mud.
qs: Where did Rob put the pig?
Rob put the pig in a pen.
How did the pig get out?
He dug a pit by the log.
How do you know Rob was not angry?
He did not get mad and he let the pig sit in the mud.

write.task: Write three facts about the pig from the story. Start with a sentence that tells your topic and finish with an ending sentence.

g3.title: The Pig in the Pen
paras: Rob kept a big pink pig in a pen beside the red barn. The pen had a strong gate and a long log across one end.
The pig had other plans. All morning he pushed his snout into the soft ground and dug, and by lunchtime there was a hole under the log.
He squeezed through it, trotted into the sunshine, and dropped himself into the wettest, blackest patch of mud on the whole farm.
Rob came running. The pig ran too, and he was faster than he looked. Rob skidded, slipped, and landed in the mud with a thud.
For a moment nobody moved. Then Rob began to grin, because he was every bit as muddy as the pig. He let the pig stay until the sun went down.
qs: What did the pen have to keep the pig in?
A strong gate and a long log across one end.
How long did it take the pig to dig the hole?
From the morning until lunchtime.
Why does the author say the pig 'was faster than he looked'?
Because Rob could not catch him and landed in the mud instead.

write.task: Write a how-to telling someone how to keep a pig in a pen. Group your steps in order and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Pig in the Pen
paras: Rob's pig was enormous and had opinions about freedom. The pen beside the red barn had a strong gate, a log across the low end, and, Rob believed, no weaknesses at all.
The pig disagreed. He spent the whole morning working his snout into the soft ground near the log, shifting a little more earth each time, patient as water wearing at stone.

By noon the hole was wide enough. He wriggled through, shook himself off, and marched directly to the deepest, blackest patch of mud on the property, where he lay down with a sigh of pure satisfaction.
Rob sprinted across the yard. The pig, who was considerably faster than an enormous pig has any right to be, swung around the mud and left Rob to skid through it alone.
Rob sat up, dripping. He looked at the pig. The pig looked back, entirely unrepentant. Rob grinned in spite of himself, then went to get a shovel, because the hole would still be there tomorrow.
qs: What comparison does the author use for how the pig dug?
Patient as water wearing at stone.
Why did Rob end up in the mud instead of the pig?
The pig swung around it and Rob skidded straight through.
What does the last sentence suggest about the pig's escape?
That it will happen again unless Rob fixes the hole.

write.task: Write the next day from the pig's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence of events, and use dialogue and sensory details.

g2.title: The Chick in the Shed
paras: Chet has a shed at the back. In the shed is a hen. The hen has one thin chick.
The chick will not eat. Chet got a dish and put mash in it. He set the dish by the chick.
The chick did not wish to eat. It just sat in the sun and did not peck.
Then Chet got a thin chip of ham. He held it up. The chick ran to him and got it!
Now the chick will eat. Chet shuts the shed. He is much better at this than he was.
qs: What is in Chet's shed?
A hen and one thin chick.
What did Chet put in the dish?
He put mash in it.
What made the chick eat?
A thin chip of ham that Chet held up.

write.task: Was the ham a good way to get the chick to eat? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Chet and the Fish
paras: Chet had one wish that summer: to catch the big fish that lived in the pond behind the shed. Everybody in the family had seen it. Nobody had ever caught it.
On Thursday he carried his rod down to the water and sat in the thin shade of a willow. He had a chip of ham on the hook and a whole afternoon ahead of him.
The sun climbed. A bug landed on his chin, and he let it stay rather than move and scare the fish. Three hours went by without one pull on the line.
Then the rod bent nearly double. Chet held on with both hands while the line hissed through the water, and at last a thick silver fish came up into the light.
He looked at it for a long moment. Then he unhooked it and slid it gently back into the pond. “I will catch you when you are bigger,” he told it.
qs: Why was this fish famous in Chet's family?
Everybody had seen it but nobody had ever caught it.
Why did Chet let the bug stay on his chin?
He did not want to move and scare the fish.
What does Chet's choice at the end tell you about him?
He is patient and willing to wait and catch it when it is bigger.

write.task: Write what happens the day Chet goes back. Use time-order words, describe the pond, and include something Chet says out loud.

g4.title: Chet and the Fish
paras: Every family keeps a story, and Chet's family kept the one about the fish in the pond behind the shed. His grandfather had hooked it twice and lost it twice. His mother claimed she had seen it rise, broad as a dinner plate, on a still evening in June.
Chet went down on a Thursday with his rod, a chip of ham, and the whole long afternoon in front of him. He settled into the thin shade of the willow and made himself a promise not to move.

Keeping that promise turned out to be the hard part. The sun pushed higher. A bug landed on his chin and walked across it, and Chet let it, because the surface of the pond was flat and perfect and he would not be the one to break it.

The strike, when it finally came, nearly took the rod out of his hands. Line hissed off the reel. His arms burned. For four full minutes the fish ran, and then it tired, and a thick silver shape rose slowly into the light.

Chet held it in the shallows, feeling the size of it, the cold muscle of it working against his palms. Then he worked the hook free and let go. The fish hung still for a second and vanished. “I will catch you when you are bigger,” Chet said, to nobody at all.
qs: What evidence shows the fish was important to Chet's whole family?
His grandfather hooked and lost it twice and his mother saw it rise.
What promise did Chet make himself, and why was it hard to keep?
Not to move, which was hard because a bug walked across his chin.
Why might the author end with 'to nobody at all'?
To show Chet is alone and the moment is private to him.

write.task: Chet released a fish his family had chased for years. Was that the right choice? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Bell on the Hill
paras: Nell has a job. The bell on the hill is hers. When it is six, Nell will hit the bell and the kids run up the path.
Then the bell fell off. It fell in the mud at the back of the mill. Nell did not yell.
She got a rag and a tub of suds. She did wash the bell until it was much bell and less mud.
Then Nell put the bell back on top of the hill. It was a big job.
At six, Nell hit the bell. The kids ran up the path. Nell will not miss.
qs: What is Nell's job?
To hit the bell on the hill when it is six.
What happened to the bell?
It fell off and landed in the mud at the back of the mill.
How did Nell fix it?
She got a rag and a tub of suds and washed it.

write.task: Write three facts about Nell's job. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Bell on the Hill
paras: Nell had the best job in the village. At six o'clock every morning she climbed the hill and rang the bell, and every child in the valley understood it was time to start walking to school.
One wet morning the rope slipped, the bracket gave way, and the bell went over the rim of the hill. It rolled all the way down and stopped in the mud behind the mill.
Nell did not panic. She fetched a rag and a bucket of soapy water, and she scrubbed until the brass came back bright enough to see her own face in.
Getting it up the hill again was the hard part. It took her until nearly six, and her arms shook the whole way.
She hung it, waited, and struck it on the hour. Down in the valley, doors began to open.
qs: What did Nell do at six o'clock every morning?
She climbed the hill and rang the bell.
What caused the bell to fall?
The rope slipped and the bracket gave way.
How do you know the village depended on Nell?
When she rang the bell, doors began to open all over the valley.

write.task: Should a child have a job like Nell's? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Bell on the Hill
paras: Nell had held the job since she was nine, and in four years she had not missed a single morning. At six she climbed the hill, took the rope in both hands, and rang the bell, and every child in the valley below understood it was time to start walking.

On a wet morning in March the rope slipped through her fingers. The bracket, rusted thin by years of rain, gave way all at once. The bell went over the lip of the hill and rolled, ringing all the way down, until it buried itself in the mud behind the mill.
Nell stood at the top and looked at the long brown scar it had left in the grass. Then she went down after it with a rag and a bucket, because nobody else was going to.
She scrubbed for an hour. Brass came up under the mud, dull at first, then bright enough to show her face stretched strange across the curve of it. Carrying it back up took everything she had.
At three minutes to six she hung it on a new bracket. At six she struck it. All down the valley, one door after another swung open, and Nell sat down in the wet grass and let her arms shake.
qs: How long had Nell held the job, and what is her record?
Since she was nine, and she had not missed a single morning in four years.
What does 'rusted thin by years of rain' explain?
Why the bracket gave way and the bell fell.
Why does the author end with Nell letting her arms shake?
To show how hard the work was, now that the job is done.

write.task: Write the scene where Nell carries the bell back up the hill. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Cave by the Lake
paras: Jane and Dave ride bikes to the lake. A cave is cut in the side of the hill. It is wide but it is not big.
Jane came up to the cave. She made a note of the time. Dave gave her a rope to hold.
Inside, Jane came to a pile of five white bones. A mole had made a home in the cave.
Jane did not take the bones. She made a note and came back out to Dave.
At home, Jane made a page in her log. She gave the cave a name. It is Mole Cave.
qs: Where is the cave?
It is cut in the side of the hill by the lake.
What did Jane find inside?
A pile of five white bones and a mole home.
What did Jane name the cave?
She gave it the name Mole Cave.

write.task: Tell what Jane did, in order. Use first, next, and last, and end by telling how Jane felt.

g3.title: The Stone Gate
paras: Jane lived at the end of a long lane, behind a stone gate so wide that two cars could have driven through it side by side.
That was the problem. The gate was lovely and the gate was far too heavy, because one person on her own could not make it slide more than a hand's width.
Jane tried a rope. She tried a pole jammed in the gap, leaning on it with her whole body until her feet skidded in the gravel.
Dave came up the lane while she was still leaning. He took one side, she took the other, and together they walked it closed in about four seconds.
They sat on the wall afterwards and shared a ripe plum. “Some things are not a one-person job,” Dave said.
qs: How wide was the gate?
Wide enough for two cars to drive through side by side.
Name two things Jane tried before Dave arrived.
She tried a rope and a pole jammed in the gap.
What is the lesson Dave states at the end?
Some things are not a one-person job.

write.task: Explain how to move something too heavy to lift alone. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Stone Gate
paras: Jane's home sat at the end of a lane so long that visitors usually gave up and turned around. The stone gate at the entrance had been built two hundred years earlier, when people apparently had more hands.

It was a beautiful thing, pale and heavy, carved at the top with a pattern nobody could name any more. It was also, for one eleven-year-old, completely impossible. On her own she could move it a hand's width before it stopped dead.

She tried a rope first, looping it through the ironwork and hauling until the fibres bit into her palms. Then she jammed a pole in the gap and leaned her whole body against it. Her feet skidded in the gravel. The gate did not care.

Dave came up the lane while she was still leaning, red-faced and furious. He did not say anything clever. He just took the far side, nodded at her, and the two of them walked the gate closed in about four seconds.
They sat on the wall afterwards and split a ripe plum between them, and Jane thought about how long she had been treating a two-person job as proof that she was weak.
qs: Why does the author mention the gate was built two hundred years earlier?
To suggest it was built when more people were available to move it.
What does 'The gate did not care' tell you?
That no amount of Jane's effort alone would move it.
What does Jane realise at the end?
That needing help was not proof she was weak, because it was a two-person job.

write.task: Is asking for help a sign of weakness? Group your reasons, support them with details from the story, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Frog Jump
paras: Fran has a frog. The frog is Spot. Spot can jump up on a stump.
The class had a frog jump. Ten frogs sat on a flat rock in the grass.
Stan had a frog that went fast. It went past Spot in one jump.
Then Spot bent his legs. He made a big jump and went past Stan's frog.
Spot won the frog jump. Fran held him up. The class clapped and Spot sat still.
qs: What is the frog's name?
The frog is Spot.
Where did the ten frogs sit?
On a flat rock in the grass.
How did Spot win?
He bent his legs and made a big jump past Stan's frog.

write.task: Which frog was best, Spot or Stan's frog? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Frog Jump
paras: Fran had kept a frog named Spot in a tank by the window since spring. He was small, green, and spent most of his life sitting absolutely still on a stump.
In June the class held a frog jump. Ten frogs were set on a flat rock in the grass, and ten children knelt behind them shouting encouragement.
Stan's frog went first and went fast, clearing the chalk line in one flat leap. Everyone agreed that was that.
Spot did nothing for a long moment. Then he folded his back legs under him, held still one second more, and sprang clean past Stan's mark.
Fran lifted him up and the class clapped. Spot, who had no idea he had won anything, sat perfectly still in her hands.
qs: Where had Fran kept Spot since spring?
In a tank by the window.
Why did everyone think Stan's frog had won?
It cleared the chalk line in a single flat leap.
What is funny about Spot at the end?
He won but had no idea he had won anything.

write.task: Write the frog jump from Spot's point of view. Use time-order words and include what the noise felt like.

g4.title: The Frog Jump
paras: Fran had kept Spot since spring, in a glass tank on the windowsill where the afternoon light came through. He was a small green frog with an enormous talent for doing nothing at all, and he practised it daily on a piece of driftwood she had put in for him.

The class frog jump was held in June on the flat rock behind the school. Ten frogs, ten lines of chalk, ten children kneeling in the grass and shouting advice that no frog has ever been able to follow.

Stan's frog went first. It was long-legged and quick, and it cleared the chalk in one flat leap that pulled a gasp from everybody watching. Stan folded his arms. The contest, as far as he was concerned, was finished.

Spot sat. He sat so long that children began to laugh. Fran crouched beside him and said nothing, because she had watched him on that driftwood all spring and she had learned the difference between a frog who would not jump and a frog who was not ready yet.

He folded his back legs. He waited one second longer. Then he went, high and clean, over Stan's chalk line with room to spare. The class erupted. Spot, who understood none of it, settled into Fran's cupped hands and went back to doing nothing at all.
qs: What had Fran learned from watching Spot all spring?
The difference between a frog who will not jump and one who is not ready yet.
How does the author show Stan was overconfident?
He folded his arms and considered the contest finished.
Why is it funny that Spot 'understood none of it'?
Because everyone else is celebrating a victory the frog cannot even know about.

write.task: Write a short report on frogs for a younger reader. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Rain on Game Day
paras: Gail and Ray play on the same side. The big game was set for Saturday.
Then the rain came. It fell all day and it did not stay away.
The field was wet. The trail to it was just mud. Will the game wait?
Gail got a rake. Ray got a bag of sand. They did not wait for help. They made a dry way to the field.
At ten the sun came up and the game was on. Gail and Ray had mud on them, but they did play.
qs: When was the big game set for?
It was set for Saturday.
What was wrong with the trail to the field?
It was just mud because the rain fell all day.
How did Gail and Ray fix it?
Gail got a rake and Ray got a bag of sand, and they made a dry way.

write.task: Should the game have been played in the mud? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Rain on Game Day
paras: Gail and Ray had been waiting all season for the Saturday game, and on Friday night the rain started and did not stop.
By morning the field was a swamp. The trail down to it had turned to thick brown mud that pulled at your shoes.
The coach said the game might be called off. Gail did not want to wait around to find out, so she went home and came back with a rake.
Ray arrived ten minutes later dragging a bag of sand. They worked along the trail, raking and spreading, until there was a dry way to walk on.
The sun came out at ten and the game went ahead. Both of them played the whole match with mud up to their knees, and not one of them complained.
qs: When did the rain start?
On Friday night, and it did not stop.
What did Gail and Ray each bring?
Gail brought a rake and Ray brought a bag of sand.
Why do you think neither of them complained about the mud?
Because they had worked to make sure the game could be played at all.

write.task: Write what happened on the trail that morning. Use time-order words, describe what the mud was like, and include dialogue.

g4.title: Rain on Game Day
paras: Gail and Ray had been waiting for the Saturday game since the season began. On Friday night the rain arrived, and it settled in over the valley with no intention of leaving.

By morning the field had become a swamp and the trail leading down to it was thick brown mud that gripped your shoes and held on. The coach stood at the top of it with his arms crossed, saying the word postponed.

Gail did not stay to argue. She walked home, took the rake off the wall of the shed, and walked back, and by the time she returned Ray was coming the other way dragging a bag of sand he had talked out of the groundskeeper.
They worked the whole length of the trail. Rake, spread, press down, move on. It was slow and it was filthy and not one of them suggested stopping, because stopping meant no game.

At ten the clouds broke apart and the sun came through, and the coach, who had been watching the last part of this from the clubhouse window, called them on. Gail and Ray played the full match with mud to their knees and never once mentioned the trail to anybody.
qs: What word was the coach saying at the top of the trail?
Postponed.
How did Ray get the bag of sand?
He talked the groundskeeper out of it.
Why might they never mention the trail to anybody?
They did the work to play, not to be praised for it.

write.task: Did Gail and Ray do the right thing by fixing the trail themselves? Group your reasons, use details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Seed Team
paras: Dean and Lee had a tray of seeds. They put each seed in a pot of dirt.
Each day they gave them a drink. The seeds did not seem to get big.
Lee said, “We need heat.” They set the pots near the glass where the sun is.
In a week, green leaves came up. Dean and Lee were pleased.
They had a real team of plants. Each pot got a name on a bit of tape.
qs: What did Dean and Lee put in each pot?
They put a seed in a pot of dirt.
What did Lee say the seeds need?
Lee said they need heat.
What came up in a week?
Green leaves came up.

write.task: Write three facts about how to grow a seed. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Seed Team
paras: Dean and Lee started with a tray of bean seeds and a bag of dirt, and a plan to grow something before the end of the term.
They planted one seed in each pot and watered them every day without fail. For two weeks nothing happened at all. The dirt just sat there looking like dirt.
“They need heat,” Lee said at last. So they carried the whole tray over to the window where the afternoon sun came through the glass.
Four days later the first green leaf pushed up through the dirt, and then another, and by the end of the week every pot had something growing in it.
They labelled each one with tape and a marker. Dean wanted to call them all Steve. Lee talked him out of it.
qs: What kind of seeds did they start with?
Bean seeds.
How long did nothing happen?
Two weeks.
What was Lee's idea, and did it work?
To move them to the window for heat, and yes, leaves came up four days later.

write.task: Write a how-to for growing a bean seed. Group your steps, use topic words like seed, soil and sunlight, and put them in order.

g4.title: The Seed Team
paras: Dean and Lee began the project in October with a tray of bean seeds, a bag of potting soil, and a shared determination to grow something before the term ended.

They were careful. One seed per pot, pressed down to the depth the packet recommended, watered every single day without fail. And for two solid weeks, absolutely nothing happened. The soil sat there looking exactly like soil.

Lee worked out the problem on a cold Thursday. “They need heat,” she said. “We have been keeping them in the coldest corner of the room.” They carried the entire tray across to the window, where the afternoon sun came through the glass and warmed the sills.
The first leaf appeared four days later, pale green and folded over on itself like something learning how to stand. By Friday there was one in every pot.

They labelled each plant with tape and a marker. Dean proposed naming all of them Steve, on the grounds that it would be easier to remember. Lee pointed out, reasonably, that this would make the record-keeping meaningless, and they settled on numbers.
qs: What two mistakes had the pair not made before the leaves appeared?
They planted at the right depth and watered every day without fail.
What did Lee realise was wrong?
The seeds were in the coldest corner of the room and needed heat.
What image does the author use for the first leaf?
Something learning how to stand.

write.task: Write a report on what a seed needs to grow. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Slow Boat
paras: Joan has a boat. It is slow. It will not go fast, and Joan likes it that way.
She rows down the stream. A crow sits on the bow and will not go.
By the road Joan sees a goat. The goat has its coat in a bush and is stuck.
Joan rows to the bank. She gets the coat free and the goat runs up the slope.
The crow stays all the way back. Joan says that crow may own the boat by now.
qs: What is Joan's boat like?
It is slow and will not go fast.
What sits on the bow?
A crow sits on the bow.
What was wrong with the goat?
Its coat was stuck in a bush by the road.

write.task: Tell what Joan did, in order. Use first, next, and last, and end by telling how Joan felt.

g3.title: The Slow Boat
paras: Joan's boat was the slowest on the whole stream, and she had no plans to change that. She liked having time to look at things.
She rowed out after breakfast with a crow riding on the bow. It had taken up that spot three weeks earlier and showed no sign of giving it up.
Near the road she spotted a goat tangled in a thorn bush, its coat caught fast on both sides. It had clearly been struggling for a while.
Joan rowed to the bank, climbed out, and worked the coat loose a thorn at a time, talking quietly the whole while so the goat would hold still.
The goat bolted up the slope the moment it was free. The crow had not moved an inch. Joan had begun to suspect the boat belonged to it now.
qs: Why did Joan like a slow boat?
She liked having time to look at things.
How long had the crow been riding on the bow?
Three weeks.
Why did Joan talk quietly while freeing the goat?
So the goat would hold still.

write.task: Write the goat's side of this story. Develop the character, use time-order words, and include what it could see and hear.

g4.title: The Slow Boat
paras: Joan's boat was the slowest thing on the stream and she had no intention of improving it. A fast boat gets you to the end. A slow one lets you see what you are passing, which was, as far as Joan was concerned, the entire point.
She rowed out after breakfast with a crow riding the bow. It had claimed the position three weeks earlier, and it now treated her presence as a minor inconvenience to be tolerated.
Near the road she saw the goat. It was tangled in a thorn bush, its coat caught on both sides, and from the state of the ground it had been fighting the bush for most of the morning and losing.

Joan tied up, climbed the bank, and began working the coat free one thorn at a time. She talked the whole while, low and steady and about nothing in particular, because an animal that is listening to a voice is not thrashing against thorns.

The goat went up the slope the instant it was loose, without a backward glance. The crow had not shifted an inch through any of it. Joan pushed off, took up the oars, and privately conceded that the boat was probably the crow's now.
qs: What is Joan's argument for a slow boat?
A fast boat gets you to the end but a slow one lets you see what you are passing.
How could Joan tell the goat had been stuck a long time?
From the state of the ground where it had been fighting the bush.
Why did Joan keep talking while she worked?
An animal listening to a voice is not thrashing against the thorns.

write.task: Is it better to travel slowly or quickly? Group your reasons, support them with facts and details, and finish with a conclusion.

g2.title: Go, Bo, Go
paras: Bo is my pup. Bo is red. He can go and go and go.
We go up to the top of the lot. Bo digs. He digs a pit by a log.
I say, “No, Bo. We can not dig a pit by the log.”
Bo sits. He is sad. So I give him a pat. He is not sad a lot.
We go to the van. Bo is on my lap. He is my pup and I am his.
qs: Who is Bo?
Bo is my red pup.
Where does Bo dig a pit?
He digs a pit by a log.
How do you know Bo does not stay sad?
He is not sad a lot and he sits on my lap.

write.task: Tell what Bo did, in order. Use first, next, and last, and end by telling how Bo felt.

g3.title: Go, Bo, Go
paras: Bo is a red pup with one white foot and no sense of when to stop running.
We walk him to the top of the empty lot every morning, and every morning he finds the same log and starts digging beside it.
“No, Bo,” I tell him. “Not there.” He looks up with dirt on his nose and thinks about it.
He sits down then, properly sad, ears flat. It lasts about four seconds, which is as long as Bo has ever been sad about anything.
By the time we get back to the van he has forgotten the whole thing. He rides home on my lap with his chin on my arm.
qs: What does Bo do every morning at the lot?
He digs beside the same log.
How long does Bo stay sad?
About four seconds.
What does the last line show about Bo and the narrator?
That they are close, because Bo rides on the narrator's lap.

write.task: Explain how to take a dog for a walk. Group your steps in order and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Go, Bo, Go
paras: Bo is a red pup with one white foot, an excellent nose, and absolutely no sense of when a thing is finished. He does not walk anywhere. He arrives.

Every morning we take him to the empty lot at the top of the road, and every morning, out of all the ground available to him, he chooses the same log and begins digging beside it with real conviction.

“No, Bo,” I tell him. “Not there.” He stops. He looks up with dirt across the bridge of his nose and considers the instruction carefully, the way you might consider a suggestion from someone who has never dug anything in their life.
Then he sits, and he is sad. Ears flat, chin low, the full performance. It lasts about four seconds, which is the longest Bo has ever been sad about anything, including the time he fell in the creek.
By the time we reach the van he has forgotten all of it. He rides home across my lap with his chin hooked over my arm, already asleep, already planning tomorrow's hole.
qs: What does 'He does not walk anywhere. He arrives.' tell you about Bo?
That he moves fast and with energy rather than calmly.
How does the author describe the way Bo considers the instruction?
Like a suggestion from someone who has never dug anything in their life.
Why does the author call Bo's sadness a performance?
Because it lasts only four seconds and is not really felt.

write.task: Should dogs be allowed to dig wherever they want? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Red Hen
paras: Peg has a hen. The hen is red. Peg put the hen in a pen.
The hen got out. It ran to the mud by the tub. It did not go in the pen.
Peg got a bit of a bun. She put the bit in the pen.
The hen ran in to get the bun. Peg got the pen set.
Now the hen is in the pen. Peg is not mad. She is a bit wet, but the hen is in.
qs: What did Peg put in the pen?
She put a bit of a bun in the pen.
Where did the hen go when it got out?
It ran to the mud by the tub.
Why did Peg use the bun?
To get the hen to run back in the pen.

write.task: Was the bun a good way to catch the hen? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Red Hen
paras: Peg kept one red hen, and the red hen kept getting out. The pen had been mended three times already that month.
One morning it was out again, standing in the mud by the water tub and refusing, politely, to come anywhere near her.
Peg had learned not to chase it. Chasing made it faster. Instead she went inside, tore a piece off a bun, and set it down just inside the pen gate.
The hen watched her from the mud. Then it crossed the yard, walked in after the bun, and Peg closed the gate behind it.
Peg stood there, muddy to the knees, and decided that mending the pen a fourth time could wait until after lunch.
qs: How many times had the pen been mended that month?
Three times already.
Why did Peg stop chasing the hen?
Chasing only made it faster.
What does Peg decide at the end?
That mending the pen again could wait until after lunch.

write.task: Write a how-to for catching a loose chicken. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Red Hen
paras: Peg kept one red hen, and the red hen kept getting out. By the middle of the month the pen had been mended three separate times, each repair more inventive than the last, and each of them defeated inside a week.
One morning the hen was standing in the mud beside the water tub, entirely at ease, declining in the politest possible way to come within ten feet of her.

Peg had learned the hard way not to chase it. Chasing it made it faster and made her slower, and the one time she had cornered it against the fence she had gone home with a cut across her wrist and no hen.
So she went inside instead. She tore a piece off yesterday's bun, carried it out, and set it on the ground just inside the open gate. Then she stepped back and waited, saying nothing at all.

The hen considered the bun for a long moment. Then it crossed the yard at its own unhurried pace, walked through the gate, and began to eat. Peg shut the gate, looked down at the mud to her knees, and decided the fourth repair could wait until after lunch.
qs: What happened the one time Peg cornered the hen?
She went home with a cut across her wrist and no hen.
Why does Peg step back and say nothing?
So the hen will come to the bun on its own instead of being chased.
What does the repeated mending suggest about the hen?
That it is determined and keeps finding new ways out.

write.task: Write this morning from the hen's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence of events, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Jack the Duck
paras: Nick has a duck. The duck is Jack. Jack sits on a rock in the sun.
Jack will not get up. Nick can not get him up. Jack just sits.
Nick picks up a sack. In the sack is a bit of a bun.
Jack got up! He hops off the rock. He pecks at the bun in the sack.
Nick pats Jack on the back. Jack is a duck. Jack got his bun.
qs: Where does Jack sit?
Jack sits on a rock in the sun.
What is in the sack?
A bit of a bun.
What made Jack get off the rock?
The bun in the sack.

write.task: Tell what Nick did to get Jack off the rock. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Jack the Duck
paras: Nick's duck is called Jack, and Jack has one favourite rock. He sits on it most of the day, facing the sun, ignoring everybody.
Calling him does nothing. Nick has tried it for a whole summer. Jack hears his name perfectly well and simply does not move.
What does work is the sack. Nick fetched it from the shed, put a scoop of mash in the bottom, and shook it once.
Jack was off the rock before the sound finished. He crossed the yard at speed and had his head in the sack within seconds.
Nick patted him on the back while he ate. Jack is not a difficult duck, Nick has decided. He just has conditions.
qs: What is Jack's favourite spot?
One particular rock, facing the sun.
How long has Nick tried calling him?
A whole summer.
What does Nick mean by saying Jack 'has conditions'?
Jack will come, but only for the mash in the sack.

write.task: Is Jack a good pet? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Jack the Duck
paras: Nick's duck is called Jack, and Jack has one rock. Not a favourite rock among several — one rock, selected years ago for reasons known only to him, and occupied for most of every daylight hour.

Calling his name accomplishes nothing whatsoever. Nick spent an entire summer establishing this. Jack hears perfectly. He turns his head very slightly, registers that he has been addressed, and then does not move, which is somehow worse than not hearing at all.

What works is the sack. It lives on a hook in the shed, and the sound it makes when it is shaken with mash in the bottom is, as far as Jack is concerned, the only noise in the world worth responding to.
Nick shook it once. Jack was off the rock before the sound had finished, across the yard at a speed that his usual behaviour gives no hint of, and head-down in the sack within seconds.
Nick patted his back while he ate. Jack is not a difficult duck, Nick has concluded after some years of study. He simply has conditions, and he sees no reason to pretend otherwise.
qs: Why does the author correct 'favourite rock' to 'one rock'?
To show Jack uses only that rock and no other.
Why is Jack's response to his name 'worse than not hearing at all'?
Because he hears, registers it, and still refuses to move.
What is the only sound Jack responds to?
The sack being shaken with mash in the bottom.

write.task: Write a report on keeping ducks. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Fox in the Box
paras: Rex is a fox. Rex sits in a box at the back of the shed.
A quick bug got in the box. Rex did not want it in with him.
Rex got up. He did a quick dash at the bug.
The bug ran. Rex ran. The box tips on its top.
Now Rex has no box. He sits in a sack. Rex is a fox in a sack.
qs: Where does Rex sit at the start?
Rex sits in a box at the back of the shed.
What got in the box?
A quick bug got in the box.
Why does Rex end up in a sack?
The box tipped over when he dashed at the bug.

write.task: Tell what happened to the box, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Fox in the Box
paras: Rex is a small red fox who lives at the back of our shed, in a wooden box that used to hold apples.
On Saturday a quick brown beetle got into the box with him. Rex does not share. He made that clear at once.
He sprang up, missed the beetle entirely, and knocked the whole box onto its side with a crash that pulled my mother to the window.
The beetle left. Rex stood in the wreckage looking extremely surprised, which is not a thing foxes are good at hiding.
He sleeps in a feed sack now. It is softer than the box was, and so far nothing has crawled into it.
qs: What did the box used to hold?
Apples.
What happened when Rex sprang at the beetle?
He missed it and knocked the box onto its side.
Why is the sack better than the box?
It is softer and nothing has crawled into it.

write.task: Should wild animals be allowed to live near a house? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Fox in the Box
paras: Rex is a small red fox who has lived at the back of our shed since the spring before last, in a wooden crate that used to hold apples and still, faintly, smells of them.

On Saturday a beetle got in with him. It was an ordinary beetle, brown and unhurried, and it had no particular intentions, but Rex does not share his crate with anything and he established this position immediately.

He sprang. He missed by a considerable margin. His back legs caught the edge of the crate on the way down and the whole thing went over sideways with a crash that pulled my mother to the kitchen window in about two seconds.
The beetle, which had not asked for any of this, walked away unharmed. Rex stood in the wreckage of his own home looking profoundly surprised — an expression foxes are famously bad at concealing.
He has been sleeping in a feed sack ever since. It is softer than the crate, it holds the shape of him, and so far nothing whatsoever has crawled into it.
qs: How long has Rex lived behind the shed?
Since the spring before last.
What does the author say about the beetle's intentions?
It had no particular intentions and had not asked for any of this.
What is funny about the phrase 'the wreckage of his own home'?
Rex destroyed his own crate himself while attacking a harmless beetle.

write.task: Write a report on foxes for a younger reader. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Six Hats
paras: Mom has six hats. The hats sit on a shelf in the hall.
Jen picks a hat. It flops on her nose. She can not see.
Dad grabs the next hat. It fits on him, but it is red with dots.
The pups get the last hat. They drag it to the rug and sit on it.
Mom gets the hat back. She puts the hats on the shelf. Then she picks the red one with dots.
qs: Where do the hats sit?
The hats sit on a shelf in the hall.
What happened when Jen picked a hat?
It flopped on her nose and she could not see.
Which hat does Mom pick at the end?
She picks the red one with dots.

write.task: Which hat is the best one? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: Six Hats
paras: There are six hats on the shelf in our hall, and every one of them belongs to Mom. That has never stopped anybody.
Jen tried the straw one first. It came down over her nose and she walked into the door frame, which settled the question of whether it fit.
Dad took the next one off the shelf and put it on without looking. It fit him perfectly. It was also pink and covered in white dots, and he wore it for the rest of the afternoon.
The pups got the last hat off the chair somehow, dragged it onto the rug, and sat on it together, which is how most things in our house end.
Mom got it back, brushed it off, and put all six hats in a row on the shelf. Then she took down the pink one with the dots and wore it to the shops.
qs: Who do all six hats belong to?
They all belong to Mom.
How did Jen find out the straw hat did not fit?
It came down over her nose and she walked into the door frame.
What does Mom do at the very end?
She takes the pink hat with dots and wears it to the shops.

write.task: Write about a time something did not fit. Use time-order words and include something somebody said.

g4.title: Six Hats
paras: There are six hats on the shelf in our hall. All six belong to Mom. This has never once stopped anybody in this house from wearing them.

Jen went first, as Jen always does, and chose the straw one. It came down over her nose and most of her chin, and she walked directly into the door frame, which answered the question of fit without anybody having to say anything.

Dad reached up without looking and took the next one down. It fit him perfectly, which was unfortunate, because it was pink and covered in small white dots. He wore it for the remainder of the afternoon and refused every opportunity to take it off.

The pups managed the last hat on their own. We never established how they got it off the chair. They dragged it across the floor, arranged themselves on top of it, and went to sleep, which is how a great many objects in this house finish their lives.

Mom retrieved it, brushed it out, and set all six back in a row on the shelf in the order she likes them. Then she took the pink one with the dots back down and wore it to the shops, and nobody said a word.
qs: Why does the author call Dad's perfect fit 'unfortunate'?
Because the hat was pink and covered in small white dots.
What does the author never establish about the pups?
How they got the hat off the chair.
Why might nobody say a word when Mom wears the pink hat?
Because everyone had already worn her hats without asking.

write.task: Should people be allowed to borrow things without asking? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: Ben's Bike
paras: Ben's bike is red. It has a bell and a big back rack.
Ben's dad fits a lamp on the front. Now Ben can ride when it is dim.
Ben rings the bell at the top of the lane. His pal Tess runs out.
Tess's bike is black. The two bikes go fast down the lane.
At the end they stop. Ben's hands are cold, but Ben's grin is big.
qs: What colour is Ben's bike?
Ben's bike is red.
What did Ben's dad fit on the front?
He fits a lamp on the front.
How do you know Ben had a good time?
Ben's grin is big at the end.

write.task: Tell what Ben did, in order. Use first, next, and last, and end by telling how Ben felt.

g3.title: Ben's Bike
paras: Ben's bike is red, with a bell on the handlebars and a rack over the back wheel for carrying things that will not fit in a bag.
His dad fitted a lamp to the front of it in October, which meant Ben could keep riding after the afternoons started getting dark.
He rings the bell at the top of the lane every day on his way past. It is a signal, and Tess knows it. She comes out of her gate about four seconds later.
Tess's bike is black and a little bigger than Ben's. They go down the lane together with the wind pulling at their coats, and not one of them brakes until the bottom.
At the end Ben's hands are too cold to feel the handlebars properly. He does not mention this to anybody, because tomorrow he would like to do it again.
qs: What is the rack on the back for?
Carrying things that will not fit in a bag.
Why did Ben's dad fit a lamp in October?
So Ben could keep riding after the afternoons got dark.
Why does Ben not mention his cold hands?
He wants to be allowed to do it again tomorrow.

write.task: Explain how to ride a bike safely when it is dark. Group your points and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Ben's Bike
paras: Ben's bike is red and secondhand and the best thing he owns. It has a bell bolted to the handlebars, a rack over the back wheel for the things that will not fit in a bag, and a scrape down one side that was there when he got it.

His dad fitted a lamp to the front in October. It was a small job and it took him twenty minutes, and it meant that Ben could go on riding after the afternoons started closing in at four, which is not a small thing when you are eleven.

He rings the bell once at the top of the lane on the way past. It is not decoration. It is a signal, and Tess's front gate opens about four seconds later, every single time, without either of them ever having agreed on it.

Tess's bike is black and a size bigger. They go down the lane side by side with the wind pulling at their coats and the hedges going past too fast to see properly, and neither of them touches the brakes until the bottom, which is the whole point of the lane.

At the end Ben's hands are too cold to feel the handlebars. He does not mention this to his father, or to Tess, or to anybody, because tomorrow is Saturday and he would very much like to do it all again.
qs: What three details does the author give about the bike in the first paragraph?
A bell on the handlebars, a rack over the back wheel, and a scrape down one side.
Why does the author say the bell 'is not decoration'?
Because it is a signal to Tess, who comes out four seconds later.
What is 'the whole point of the lane'?
Going down it without touching the brakes.

write.task: Write the ride down the lane from Tess's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Picnic Basket
paras: Mom packs a basket. In it is a muffin, a napkin, and a bit of ham.
We walk to the sunset spot. Dad lugs the basket up the hill.
A rabbit sits in the grass. It is not upset. It just sits and blinks at us.
We sit on a blanket and eat. The muffin is the best bit.
The sun drops. We pack up the basket and walk back in the dim.
qs: What is in the basket?
A muffin, a napkin, and a bit of ham.
What sits in the grass?
A rabbit sits in the grass.
What is the best bit of the picnic?
The muffin is the best bit.

write.task: Write three facts about the picnic. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Picnic Basket
paras: Mom packed the basket herself on Sunday: muffins, napkins, a slab of ham, and a jar of pickles nobody had asked for.
We walked out to the spot at the top of the hill where you can see the whole valley, and Dad carried the basket the entire way without complaining once.
There was a rabbit sitting in the grass when we arrived. It did not run. It watched us spread the blanket, decided we were not a problem, and went back to eating.
The muffins were the best part, and the pickles were, as predicted, left in the jar.
We packed up when the sun went down and walked home in the dim with the empty basket swinging between us.
qs: What did Mom pack that nobody asked for?
A jar of pickles.
Why did the rabbit stay?
It decided we were not a problem.
What happened to the pickles?
They were left in the jar.

write.task: Write about a meal outdoors. Use time-order words, describe what you could see, and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Picnic Basket
paras: Mom packed the basket herself on Sunday morning and would not let anybody check it. Muffins, napkins, a slab of ham wrapped in paper, and a jar of pickles that nobody in the history of this family has ever requested.

We walked out to the spot at the very top of the hill, where the whole valley opens up below you and the wind never quite stops. Dad carried the basket the entire way, both hands, no complaints, and set it down as if it had been nothing.

A rabbit was already there, sitting in the long grass about ten feet from where we spread the blanket. It did not run. It watched the whole operation with great attention, arrived at some private conclusion about our intentions, and went back to eating.

The muffins were the best thing in the basket and disappeared first. The ham went next. The pickles sat in their jar in the middle of the blanket for two hours, exactly as everybody had privately predicted, and came home again unopened.
We packed up as the sun dropped behind the far ridge and walked back down in the half dark, the empty basket swinging between us, nobody saying very much.
qs: What does the author say about the pickles' history in the family?
Nobody has ever requested them.
How does the author show the hill is high and exposed?
The whole valley opens up below and the wind never quite stops.
What does 'arrived at some private conclusion' suggest about the rabbit?
That it decided for itself the people were not dangerous.

write.task: Is it better to eat outdoors or indoors? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Cupcake Contest
paras: Our class has a cupcake contest. One kid, one cupcake.
Mandy makes a cupcake with a lime on top. It is bumpy but it smells fine.
Hudson makes one that is the size of his fist. He had to use a big pan.
Miss Hopkins picks Mandy's lime cupcake. Mandy did not expect it at all.
Mandy cuts it up so that the whole class can taste it. That was the best bit.
qs: How many cupcakes can each kid make?
One kid, one cupcake.
What is on top of Mandy's cupcake?
A lime is on top.
What does Mandy do when she wins?
She cuts it up so the whole class can taste it.

write.task: Should the judge have picked Mandy's cupcake? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Cupcake Contest
paras: Our class held a cupcake contest in May. One cupcake each, baked at home, judged on Friday by whoever happened to be free.
Mandy made one with a slice of lime set on top. It was lopsided and the icing had slid down one side, but the whole room could smell it from the door.
Hudson made one about the size of his own fist. He had used a cake tin instead of a cupcake tray and had decided, correctly, that nobody had said he could not.
The judge picked Mandy's. Mandy, who had entered mostly because everyone else was entering, looked completely astonished.
Then she cut it into about fifteen pieces so the whole class got a taste, which most of us agreed was the best part of the afternoon.
qs: When was the contest judged?
On Friday.
Why was Hudson's cupcake so big?
He used a cake tin instead of a cupcake tray.
Why was Mandy astonished to win?
She had entered mostly because everyone else was entering.

write.task: Write a how-to for running a class contest. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Cupcake Contest
paras: Our class held a cupcake contest in May. The rules were short: one cupcake each, baked at home, judged on Friday afternoon by whichever adult could be persuaded into the room.

Mandy's had a slice of lime set on the top. It was visibly lopsided, the icing had slid down one side and set there, and it was, without any question, the best thing in the room, because you could smell it from the doorway before you could see it.

Hudson's was approximately the size of his own fist. He had used a cake tin rather than a cupcake tray, on the entirely defensible grounds that nobody had said he could not, and he presented it with the confidence of a person who knows he has found a loophole.

The judge picked Mandy's, and Mandy looked astonished. She had entered because everybody else was entering, and she told me afterwards that she had assumed the lime was a mistake right up until the moment it was not.

Then she cut it into about fifteen uneven pieces so that the whole class got a taste. Most of us agreed afterwards that this was the best part of the afternoon, and several of us noticed that she gave the biggest piece to Hudson.
qs: What were the three rules of the contest?
One cupcake each, baked at home, judged on Friday.
On what grounds did Hudson use a cake tin?
Nobody had said he could not.
What does giving Hudson the biggest piece show about Mandy?
That she was generous to the person she had beaten.

write.task: Write the contest from Hudson's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: Unpack the Van
paras: We are at the camp. Dad tells us to unpack the van.
I undo the straps. Ross unpacks the tent and the pots.
The tent is a mess. It is unfit for a dog, Ross says.
We unfold it on the grass. Bit by bit it stands up.
It is not a bad tent. It was just unpacked in a rush.
qs: What does Dad tell them to do?
He tells them to unpack the van.
What does Ross say about the tent?
He says it is unfit for a dog.
Why did the tent look like a mess at first?
It was just unpacked in a rush.

write.task: Tell how the tent got put up, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Unpack the Van
paras: We got to the campsite at four and Dad told us to unpack the van before anybody sat down, which is the rule and has always been the rule.
I undid the straps on the roof box. Ross hauled out the tent, the pots, and a bag of things nobody could identify.
The tent, when it came out of its sack, looked like something that had been rolled up wet and left in a cupboard. Ross said it was unfit for a dog.
We unfolded it anyway, on the flattest bit of grass we could find, and pegged the corners one at a time until it slowly stood itself up.
It turned out to be a perfectly good tent. It had just been packed in a hurry at the end of last summer and left that way for a year.
qs: What is the family rule on arriving?
Unpack the van before anybody sits down.
What did Ross say about the tent?
That it was unfit for a dog.
Why did the tent look so bad?
It had been packed in a hurry last summer and left for a year.

write.task: Explain how to put up a tent. Group your steps in order and use topic words like pegs, poles and groundsheet.

g4.title: Unpack the Van
paras: We reached the campsite at four in the afternoon and Dad told us to unpack the van before anybody sat down. This is the rule. It has been the rule since before I can remember, and the one time we broke it we were still unpacking at nine o'clock at night in the rain.

I undid the straps on the roof box, which had seized up over the winter and had to be worked loose a notch at a time. Ross hauled out the tent, the pots, two folding chairs, and a canvas bag that nobody could identify and nobody was willing to open.

The tent came out of its sack in one damp lump. It looked like something that had been rolled up wet and forgotten in the back of a cupboard, which is exactly what had happened to it. Ross held it at arm's length and announced that it was unfit for a dog.

We unfolded it anyway. We found the flattest piece of grass on the site, spread it out, and pegged the corners one at a time, and after about twenty minutes of nothing happening at all it suddenly stood itself up and became a tent again.
It is a perfectly good tent. It had simply been packed in a hurry on the last morning of last summer, by people who wanted to be home, and then left exactly that way for a year.
qs: What happened the one time the family broke the rule?
They were still unpacking at nine at night in the rain.
Why could the roof box straps not be undone quickly?
They had seized up over the winter.
Who does the author blame for the state of the tent?
The people who packed it in a hurry on the last morning of last summer.

write.task: Should families have rules like unpacking before resting? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Pink Ring
paras: Gran has a pink ring. She puts it in a tin on the sink.
One time the ring is not in the tin. Gran thinks and thinks.
I check the sink. I check under the rug. No ring.
Then a clink! The ring is stuck in the sink, and it winks up at me.
Gran thanks me. She puts the ring back in the tin and we both sing.
qs: Where does Gran put the ring?
She puts it in a tin on the sink.
Where was the ring stuck?
It was stuck in the sink.
What sound led to the ring?
A clink.

write.task: Tell how the ring was found, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Pink Ring
paras: Gran keeps her pink ring in a tin beside the kitchen sink, and she has kept it there for longer than I have been alive.
On Sunday the tin was empty. Gran stood very still for a moment, the way people do when they are trying not to be worried in front of somebody.
We looked everywhere. Under the rug, down the back of the chair, in the pockets of three coats. Nothing.
Then I heard a small clink when I ran the tap, and there it was, wedged just inside the drain, catching the light every time the water moved.
Gran thanked me about six times. She put it back in the tin, and then she moved the tin to the shelf, which she should have done years ago.
qs: How long has the ring been kept in the tin?
Longer than the narrator has been alive.
How did Gran react when the tin was empty?
She stood very still, trying not to look worried.
What did Gran do differently at the end?
She moved the tin to the shelf instead of beside the sink.

write.task: Where is the safest place to keep something precious? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Pink Ring
paras: Gran keeps her pink ring in a small tin on the windowsill beside the kitchen sink. It has lived there since before I was born, and the tin is older than the ring, which tells you something about how this family stores things.

On Sunday morning the tin was empty. Gran did not say anything at all for a moment. She just stood there holding the lid, very still, in the particular way that people stand when they are working hard at not being worried in front of a child.

We searched the whole downstairs. Under the rug, down the back of the armchair, through the pockets of three coats that had not been worn since March. We found a bus ticket, two buttons and a key that fits nothing, and no ring.
Then I turned the tap on to wash my hands and heard a small bright clink, and there it was, wedged just inside the mouth of the drain, catching the light every single time the water moved over it.

Gran thanked me about six times, which was five more than necessary. She dried the ring, put it back in its tin, and then carried the tin across the kitchen and set it on the high shelf, where she says she should have put it about fifteen years ago.
qs: What does the age of the tin tell you about the family?
That they keep things for a very long time.
What did they find while searching, apart from the ring?
A bus ticket, two buttons and a key that fits nothing.
Why does Gran move the tin at the end?
So the ring cannot fall into the drain again.

write.task: Write about losing something important. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence of events, and use dialogue and sensory details.

g2.title: Why the Puppy Cried
paras: My puppy is Sky. She is shy and very funny.
Sky cried and cried. I did not know why.
Mom let me try to help. I gave Sky a dry rag and a bit of jelly on a dish.
Sky did not want it. Then I spot a tiny bit of glass stuck in her leg. I got it out.
Now Sky is happy. She can run and she does not cry.
qs: What is the puppy called?
The puppy is called Sky.
What was wrong with Sky?
A tiny bit of glass was stuck in her leg.
How do you know Sky feels better?
She is happy, she can run and she does not cry.

write.task: Write three facts about taking care of a puppy. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Why the Puppy Cried
paras: My puppy is called Sky. She is shy with strangers, funny with us, and normally the happiest animal in the house.
On Friday she cried for most of the morning and nobody could work out why. She would not eat and she would not settle.
Mom let me try. I took her a dry towel, a bowl of water and a spoonful of jelly, and she turned her head away from all three.
Then I lifted her front paw and found it: a thorn, no bigger than a grain of rice, pushed right into the soft part of the pad.
It came out in one go. Sky stopped crying before I had even put it down, and by the afternoon she was tearing around the yard as though Friday had never happened.
qs: What is Sky like normally?
Shy with strangers, funny with the family, and the happiest animal in the house.
What three things did the narrator try first?
A dry towel, a bowl of water and a spoonful of jelly.
How big was the thorn?
No bigger than a grain of rice.

write.task: Write a how-to for helping an animal that is hurt. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: Why the Puppy Cried
paras: My puppy is called Sky. She is shy with strangers and extremely funny with us, and under ordinary conditions she is the happiest animal in this house by a wide margin.

On Friday she cried from about eight in the morning until nearly noon, and not one of us could work out why. She would not eat. She would not settle anywhere. She moved from the rug to the chair to under the table and cried in all three places.

Mom let me try, mostly because she had run out of ideas herself. I took a dry towel, a bowl of fresh water, and a spoonful of the jelly that Sky is not normally allowed, and she turned her head away from every one of them, which is how I knew it was serious.

So I sat down on the floor and lifted her front paws one at a time, and on the third one I found it: a thorn no bigger than a grain of rice, pushed right into the soft pad and almost invisible until the light caught it.

It came out in a single pull. Sky stopped crying before I had finished putting it down. By two o'clock she was tearing laps around the yard at full speed, entirely recovered, with no apparent memory of the morning at all.
qs: How did the narrator know the problem was serious?
Sky refused even the jelly she is not normally allowed.
Where did Sky move to while crying?
From the rug to the chair to under the table.
Why was the thorn almost invisible?
It was tiny and only showed when the light caught it.

write.task: Should children be allowed to look after a pet on their own? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Pitcher and the Catch
paras: Mitch is the pitcher. He can pitch a fast ball at the kids on his block.
Jack steps up with the bat. He swings and misses. Then he swings again.
Crack! The ball goes up and up. Mitch watches it drop.
Patch the dog runs and makes the catch. He will not let it go.
The kids yell. Patch gets a pat and the ball gets a bit of dog spit on it.
qs: Who is the pitcher?
Mitch is the pitcher.
Who makes the catch?
Patch the dog makes the catch.
Why do the kids laugh?
Because the dog caught the ball and would not let it go.

write.task: Tell what happened in the game, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Pitcher and the Catch
paras: Mitch has been the pitcher on our block for two summers, mostly because nobody else wants to stand in the sun for an hour doing the same thing.
Jack stepped up with the bat on Saturday and missed the first two completely. He does this every single game and then acts surprised about it.
On the third one there was a crack you could hear from the end of the street, and the ball went up over the hedge and kept going.
Patch, who is not allowed to play and knows it, came out of nowhere, caught it in the air, and refused absolutely to give it back.
We chased him twice around the yard and gave up. Jack says it counts as a home run. Mitch says it counts as a catch. The argument is still going.
qs: How long has Mitch been the pitcher?
Two summers.
What does Jack do every game?
He misses the first two and then acts surprised.
Why can the argument not be settled?
Jack says it is a home run and Mitch says it is a catch.

write.task: Was it a home run or a catch? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Pitcher and the Catch
paras: Mitch has been the pitcher on our block for two summers running. This is not because he is the best at it. It is because pitching means standing in direct sun for an hour doing the same motion over and over, and nobody else has ever volunteered.

Jack came up to bat on Saturday afternoon and missed the first two pitches completely, swinging about a foot under both. He does this in every game we have ever played and then looks around afterwards as though something unexpected has happened to him.

The third one connected. There was a crack you could hear from the far end of the street, and the ball went up over Mrs Dunn's hedge on a line and simply kept going, and every one of us stood still and watched it.

Patch is not allowed to play. Patch knows he is not allowed to play. Patch came out of the side gate at full stretch, took the ball out of the air in both jaws, landed, and declined with total finality to give it back to anybody.

We chased him twice around the yard and then stopped, because it was clearly pointless and he was clearly enjoying it. Jack maintains it was a home run. Mitch maintains it was a catch. As of this week the argument has been running for eleven days.
qs: Why is Mitch the pitcher?
Because nobody else volunteers to stand in the sun doing the same motion.
What does Jack do after missing?
He looks around as though something unexpected has happened to him.
Why did they stop chasing Patch?
It was pointless and he was clearly enjoying it.

write.task: Write the catch from Patch the dog's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Storm in the Barn
paras: A storm hits the farm. The sky is dark and the wind is sharp.
Mark runs to the barn to shut it up. The corn in the cart is getting wet.
In the dark a short bark starts up. A pup is stuck under the cart.
Mark lifts the cart and the pup darts out. It is not hurt, just cross.
They sit in the barn until the storm stops. Then they walk back in the yard.
qs: What hits the farm?
A storm hits the farm.
Why does Mark run to the barn?
To shut it up, because the corn in the cart is getting wet.
What was stuck under the cart?
A pup was stuck under the cart.

write.task: Tell what Mark did in the storm, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Storm in the Barn
paras: The storm came over the farm just before dark, and you could hear it in the trees a full minute before the first of the rain arrived.
Mark ran for the barn to get the door shut. The cart was still standing in the yard with the corn on it, uncovered.
He was halfway through dragging the cover across when he heard a short, sharp bark from somewhere underneath.
It took both hands and all his strength to lift the cart far enough. The pup shot out to one side, soaked and furious, and entirely unhurt.
They sat together in the barn for an hour while the storm worked itself out. By the time they walked back across the yard, the sky had gone clear.
qs: How did Mark know the storm was coming?
He could hear it in the trees a minute before the rain.
What was wrong with the cart?
It was standing in the yard with the corn uncovered.
How was the pup when it got out?
Soaked and furious, but entirely unhurt.

write.task: Explain what to do on a farm when a storm is coming. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Storm in the Barn
paras: The storm came over the north ridge just before dark. You could hear it in the trees for a full minute before the first rain reached the yard, a long rolling sound building out of nothing, and then it arrived all at once.

Mark ran for the barn with his arms over his head. The cart was still standing in the middle of the yard with the morning's corn stacked on it and no cover over any of it, which was his fault and he knew it.
He was halfway through hauling the tarp across when he heard it: a short, sharp bark, very close, coming from somewhere underneath the cart itself. He stopped and listened. It came again.

Getting the cart up took both hands, his shoulder, and more or less all of his weight, and he had it for about four seconds. The pup came out sideways in a single movement, soaked through, extremely angry, and completely unhurt.

They sat out the rest of it together in the barn, Mark on an upturned crate and the pup pressed hard against his boot. By the time the thunder had moved off east and they walked back across the yard, the sky had gone entirely clear and the stars were out.
qs: How does the author describe the sound of the storm arriving?
A long rolling sound building out of nothing in the trees.
Why does Mark think the uncovered corn is his fault?
He had left the cart in the yard with no cover on it.
What detail shows the pup had been frightened?
It pressed hard against his boot while they sat out the storm.

write.task: Should Mark have gone under the cart to help the pup? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Gold Colt
paras: Old Mr Finch has a colt. The colt is gold and very bold.
It gets cold at dark. Mr Finch is told to hold the colt in the barn.
But the colt will not stay. It kicks the bolt and gets out in the wild grass.
We find it behind the post by the road. It is cold but it does not mind.
Mr Finch is kind. He folds a blanket on the colt and holds the rope all the way home.
qs: What colour is the colt?
The colt is gold.
How does the colt get out?
It kicks the bolt.
Where do they find the colt?
Behind the post by the road.

write.task: Should the colt be kept in the barn at night? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Gold Colt
paras: Old Mr Finch keeps one gold colt, and the colt is the boldest animal on his land by a long way.
When the nights started getting cold, the vet told him to keep it in the barn until spring. Mr Finch agreed, which was the easy part.
The colt disagreed. On the second night it worked the bolt loose with its nose and was gone before anybody heard a thing.
We found it in the morning standing behind the old post by the road, wet to the shoulder and entirely unbothered, eating the wild grass in the ditch.
Mr Finch did not shout. He folded a blanket over its back, took hold of the rope, and walked it the whole mile home without once letting go.
qs: What did the vet tell Mr Finch to do?
Keep the colt in the barn until spring.
How did the colt get out?
It worked the bolt loose with its nose.
How do you know Mr Finch is patient?
He did not shout and walked it the whole mile home.

write.task: Write the night the colt escaped from the colt's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see and hear.

g4.title: The Gold Colt
paras: Old Mr Finch keeps one gold colt on forty acres, and that colt is, by a considerable distance, the boldest animal on the property. He has had horses for fifty years and he says so himself.

When the nights began turning cold in October the vet told him to keep it stabled until spring. Mr Finch agreed without argument, which turned out to be the only straightforward part of the whole arrangement.

The colt did not agree. On the second night it spent what must have been a considerable amount of time working the bolt loose with its nose, and it was out and across the field before anybody in the house heard a single sound.

We found it the next morning standing behind the old post by the road, wet to the shoulder, steaming slightly in the early light, and entirely unbothered by any of it, working its way steadily through the wild grass in the ditch.

Mr Finch did not shout, and he did not hurry. He folded a blanket across its back, took a short hold of the rope, and walked it the entire mile home without letting go once. Then he put a second bolt on the door.
qs: How long has Mr Finch kept horses?
Fifty years.
What does 'steaming slightly in the early light' tell you?
The colt was wet and warm from standing out all night.
What does Mr Finch do after walking the colt home?
He puts a second bolt on the door.

write.task: Write a report on caring for horses in cold weather. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Knot in the Night
paras: Dwight has a kite. The string has a knot in it that he can not undo.
He sits in the light by the window and tries. His knee is sore.
Mom knows how. She has a knack with string. She takes it and twists it right.
The knot comes undone. Dwight writes his name on the kite in black.
At night he hangs it high on the wall so he can see it from his bed.
qs: What is wrong with the kite string?
It has a knot in it.
Who undoes the knot?
Mom undoes it, because she has a knack with string.
What does Dwight write on the kite?
He writes his name on it in black.

write.task: Tell how the knot got undone, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Knot in the Night
paras: Dwight got a kite for his birthday and could not fly it, because somewhere in the middle of the string there was a knot the size of a walnut.
He sat under the lamp by the window and worked at it for most of an hour. His knees went numb against the floorboards and the knot did not get any smaller.
Mom has a knack with string. She always has. She took it from him without saying anything, turned it twice in her hands, and found the one loop that mattered.
It came undone in about four seconds, which Dwight has still not entirely forgiven. He wrote his name along the spine of the kite in black marker.
That night he hung it high on his bedroom wall, where he could see the shape of it against the light from the hall.
qs: How big was the knot?
The size of a walnut.
How long did Dwight work at it?
Most of an hour.
Why has Dwight not forgiven his mother?
Because she undid in four seconds what he had worked at for an hour.

write.task: Is it better to keep trying or to ask for help? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Knot in the Night
paras: Dwight got the kite for his birthday in March and did not fly it once that month, because somewhere in the middle of two hundred feet of string there was a knot about the size of a walnut and twice as stubborn.

He sat under the lamp by the window and worked at it on four separate evenings. His knees went numb against the floorboards. He tried his fingers, then a pencil, then the point of a knife, and the knot absorbed all of it and did not get any smaller.

Mom has a knack with string, and always has had. She took it out of his hands on the Thursday without saying anything at all, turned it over twice, found the one loop in the whole arrangement that mattered, and pulled.

It came apart in under four seconds. Dwight has not entirely forgiven this and probably never will. He said nothing for a while, then went and got a black marker and wrote his name in careful letters along the spine of the kite.
That night he hung it high on his bedroom wall, above the shelf, where the light coming in from the hallway caught the edge of it and he could lie in bed and see the whole shape against the dark.
qs: What three things did Dwight try on the knot?
His fingers, then a pencil, then the point of a knife.
What does 'the knot absorbed all of it' mean?
Nothing he tried made any difference to it.
Why does Dwight say nothing for a while?
He is annoyed that his mother solved it so easily.
