write.task: Write about a problem that somebody else solved easily. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Owl in the Woods
paras: We found an owl in the woods behind our house. It was on a low branch and would not move.
Mom said to stay back. An owl can look sound but still be hurt.
We counted out loud. One, two, three. The owl did not blink.
Then it took off without a sound and went up over the trees.
We stood and looked at the empty branch for a good long moment.
qs: Where did they find the owl?
In the woods behind our house, on a low branch.
What did Mom say?
To stay back, because an owl can look sound but still be hurt.
How did the owl fly away?
It took off without a sound and went up over the trees.

write.task: Write three facts about owls from the story. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Owl in the Woods
paras: We found the owl on a low branch in the woods behind the house, about four feet off the ground and much closer than an owl should ever let you get.
Mom made us stand back. An owl can look perfectly sound and still have something broken, she said, and a frightened one will hurt you without meaning to.
So we counted out loud instead. One, two, three, four. The owl looked at us the entire time and did not blink once.
Then, with no warning and no sound whatsoever, it dropped off the branch, opened out, and went up over the tops of the trees.
We stood looking at the empty branch for a long moment afterwards. Nobody said anything. There did not seem to be much to say.
qs: How high was the branch?
About four feet off the ground.
Why did Mom make them stand back?
An owl can look sound but have something broken, and a frightened one will hurt you.
What is surprising about how the owl left?
It made no sound at all.

write.task: Write about seeing a wild animal close up. Use time-order words and describe what you could see and hear.

g4.title: The Owl in the Woods
paras: We found the owl on a low branch in the woods behind our house, about four feet off the ground and a great deal closer than any owl has business letting a person get.

Mom put an arm out and made us stand back. An owl can look perfectly sound and still have something broken inside it, she told us, and a frightened owl will put its feet through your hand without the slightest intention of doing you harm.

So we counted out loud instead, which was the only thing on offer. One, two, three, four. It looked back at us the entire time with those enormous flat yellow eyes and did not blink once in four whole minutes.
Then, with no warning at all and no sound whatsoever, it simply dropped off the branch, opened out to twice the size we had thought it was, and went up and over the tops of the trees in three beats.
We stood there afterwards looking at the empty branch for a long moment. Nobody said anything on the walk back either. There did not seem to be a great deal worth saying about it.
qs: Why does Mom say a frightened owl is dangerous?
It will put its feet through your hand without meaning harm.
What surprised them about the owl's size?
It opened out to twice the size they had thought it was.
Why does nobody speak on the walk back?
There did not seem to be anything worth saying about it.

write.task: Should people stay away from wild animals completely? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Berry Jar
paras: Perry has a berry bush by the shed. In the summer it is full of berries.
He fills a jar and carries it in. His mum is glad.
They stir the berries in a pan on the stove. The kitchen smells sweet.
Perry is sorry when the jar is done. He wants more.
Mum says there will be more next year. The bush is still there.
qs: Where is the berry bush?
By the shed.
What do they do with the berries?
They stir them in a pan on the stove.
Why is Perry sorry?
Because the jar is done and he wants more.

write.task: Tell what Perry did with the berries, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Berry Jar
paras: There is a berry bush growing against the shed, and every summer it produces more berries than anybody in this house can get through.
Perry filled a jar on Saturday and carried it in with both hands, and his mum stopped what she was doing, which she does not often do.
They stirred the berries in a pan on the stove for most of an hour. The whole kitchen smelled sweet enough to notice from the garden.
Perry was really sorry when the last of the jar went. He stood looking into it as though more might appear.
His mum told him there would be more next year. The bush is still there, after all, and it has not failed yet.
qs: How much berries does the bush produce?
More than anybody in the house can get through.
What did Perry's mum do that she does not often do?
She stopped what she was doing.
Why will there be more berries?
The bush is still there and it has not failed yet.

write.task: Write a how-to for picking and storing berries. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Berry Jar
paras: There is a berry bush growing hard against the back of the shed, and every summer without fail it produces a quantity of berries that nobody in this house has ever managed to get through before it spoils.

Perry filled a jar with it on Saturday morning and carried it in with both hands, holding it out in front of him like something breakable, and his mum stopped what she was doing to look, which is not a thing she does often or for very much.

They stirred the berries together in a wide pan on the stove for the better part of an hour, and the smell of it got out of the kitchen and across the whole garden, so that you could stand at the far wall and know exactly what was happening indoors.

Perry was really sorry when the last of that jar went, a week later. He stood holding it up to the window and looking into the bottom of it, as though more might be persuaded to appear if he waited long enough.

His mum told him there would be more next year, and she is almost certainly right. The bush is still there against the shed, older than Perry is, and in all that time it has not once failed to berries.
qs: How does Perry carry the jar?
With both hands, held out in front of him like something breakable.
How far did the smell travel?
Across the whole garden, as far as the far wall.
What evidence suggests there will be more next year?
The bush is older than Perry and has never once failed to berries.

write.task: Write about making something with a member of your family. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: The Pumpkin Contest
paras: The children in our street plant pumpkins every year.
My pumpkin is a monster. It took three of us to lift it onto the wagon.
Hamish has one that is small but perfect. It has no marks on it at all.
The teachers give the prize to Hamish. I am not upset. My pumpkin is still the biggest.
We take them both inside and make soup, and there is enough for the whole street.
qs: What do the children plant every year?
They plant pumpkins.
Why did it take three of them to lift the pumpkin?
Because it was a monster, very big.
Who wins the prize?
Hamish wins, with a small but perfect pumpkin.

write.task: Should the prize go to the biggest pumpkin or the best one? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Pumpkin Contest
paras: Every year the children on our street plant pumpkins, and every year somebody's father gets more involved than he strictly needs to.
Mine came out an absolute monster. It took three of us and a plank to get it up onto the wagon, and the wagon complained the whole way down the hill.
Hamish planted one about the size of a football. It was small, but it had not a single mark or soft patch anywhere on it, and it sat there looking like something out of a shop.
The teachers gave him the prize, and they were right to. I was not upset about it. Mine was still, by a distance, the biggest pumpkin anybody had ever grown on that street.
We took them both inside afterwards and made soup out of the pair, and there was enough of it to go round every house on the road.
qs: What happens every year besides the planting?
Somebody's father gets more involved than he needs to.
How big was Hamish's pumpkin?
About the size of a football.
Why was the narrator not upset?
Because theirs was still the biggest ever grown on the street.

write.task: Explain how to grow a pumpkin. Group your steps in order and use topic words like seed, soil and vine.

g4.title: The Pumpkin Contest
paras: Every year the children on our street plant pumpkins for the contest at the end of October, and every single year, without exception, somebody's father becomes considerably more involved in the process than anybody has asked him to be.

Mine came out an absolute monster. It took three of us, a plank and about twenty minutes of argument to get it up onto the wagon, and the wagon made a sound on the way down the hill that none of us had heard a wagon make before.

Hamish planted one about the size of a football. It was small. It was also completely without a mark, a scar, a soft patch or a blemish of any kind, and it sat on the trestle table looking like something that had been bought rather than planted.

The teachers gave him the prize, and on reflection they were entirely right to. I was not upset, or not very. Mine remained, by a considerable distance, the largest pumpkin anybody had ever managed to produce on that street.

We took the two of them indoors afterwards and made soup out of the pair, which took the whole afternoon and most of the large pan, and there was enough of it at the end to send a bowl to every house on the road.
qs: What sound did the wagon make?
A sound none of them had heard a wagon make before.
Why did Hamish's pumpkin look bought rather than planted?
It had no mark, scar, soft patch or blemish of any kind.
What does 'or not very' admit?
That the narrator was a little upset after all.

write.task: Is winning or taking part more important? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Helpful List
paras: Dad was restless. The shed was a mess and he was not sure where to start.
I made him a list. It was short and it was helpful.
Sweep the floor. Sort the nails. Hang the tools on the wall.
He worked slowly and he worked gladly. By lunch the shed was spotless.
Dad said my list was the best thing in it. I felt useful all day.
qs: Why was Dad restless?
The shed was a mess and he was not sure where to start.
What three things were on the list?
Sweep the floor, sort the nails, and hang the tools on the wall.
How did the narrator feel at the end?
Useful all day.

write.task: Write a short list of jobs for tidying a room. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Helpful List
paras: Dad had been restless about the shed for a fortnight. It was a mess, he could see it was a mess, and he could not work out where to begin.
So I made him a list. Three things, written out plainly on the back of an envelope. Sweep the floor. Sort the nails. Hang the tools on the wall.
He worked slowly, which is how he works, and he worked gladly, which is less usual. By lunchtime the floor was spotless and every tool had a hook.
The nails turned out to be the hard part. There were six years of them in one tin, and sorting them took him until three.
Afterwards he said the list had been the most helpful thing in the shed. I have never been so pleased with an envelope.
qs: How long had Dad been restless about the shed?
A fortnight.
What was the hardest job?
Sorting the nails, because there were six years of them in one tin.
What did Dad say about the list?
That it had been the most helpful thing in the shed.

write.task: Are lists useful? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Helpful List
paras: Dad had been restless about the shed for a fortnight. He would go out and stand in the doorway of it, look at the whole business for a while, and come back in again without having touched anything.

The problem was not laziness. The problem was that there was no obvious first move. So on Saturday morning I wrote him a list on the back of an envelope, three items long. Sweep the floor. Sort the nails. Hang the tools on the wall.

He worked slowly, which is how he has always worked, and he worked gladly, which is considerably less usual. By lunchtime the floor was spotless and every tool in the place was hanging off its own hook in a row.

The nails were the hard part, as it turned out. Six years of them had gone into one large tin without ever being sorted, and getting them into sizes took him from one o'clock until nearly three, sitting on an upturned bucket in the doorway.
When it was finished he came in, sat down, and said the list had been the single most helpful thing in that shed. I have never in my life been so pleased with an envelope.
qs: What would Dad do before the list existed?
Stand in the doorway, look at it, and come back in without touching anything.
What does the author say the problem was not?
Laziness — the problem was no obvious first move.
How long did the nails take, and where did he sit?
From one until nearly three, on an upturned bucket in the doorway.

write.task: Write a report on how to break a big job into small ones. Organise it into sections, develop each with examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Fastest Runner
paras: Last week our class was running races on the grass.
Bess is the fastest runner in the class. She has been winning since the first week.
But this time she was limping. She had twisted her leg the day before.
She ran anyway. She came in third and she was smiling the whole way.
The smallest kid in the class won. Bess clapped the hardest of all of us.
qs: Where was the class running?
On the grass.
What was wrong with Bess?
She was limping because she had twisted her leg.
Who won the race?
The smallest kid in the class won.

write.task: Should Bess have run with a hurt leg? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Fastest Runner
paras: Last week our class spent an afternoon running races on the grass behind the school, which happens about twice a term.
Bess is the fastest runner we have, and she has been winning everything since the first week of the year without ever making much of it.
On Thursday she was limping. She had twisted her leg coming down the steps the day before and had not told anybody about it.
She ran anyway. She came in third, which for Bess is nowhere, and she was smiling the entire way down the track.
The smallest kid in our class won, and he looked more surprised than anybody. Bess clapped harder than the rest of us put together.
qs: How often do the races happen?
About twice a term.
How did Bess hurt her leg?
She twisted it coming down the steps the day before.
What does 'third, which for Bess is nowhere' mean?
That third place is a bad result for somebody who always wins.

write.task: Write about a time somebody kept going when it was hard. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: The Fastest Runner
paras: Last week our class spent an afternoon running races on the grass behind the school. This happens about twice a term and is taken a great deal more seriously by everybody than the teachers appear to realise.

Bess is the fastest runner in our year and has been since she arrived. She has won more or less everything going for two years, and she has never once made anything of it, which is the part that makes it bearable for the rest of us.

On Thursday she was limping before the first race even started. She had twisted her leg coming down the back steps the previous afternoon and had told precisely nobody, because telling somebody would have meant not running.
She ran anyway. She finished third, which for Bess is nowhere at all, and she was smiling the whole way down the track, and the smile was not the kind you put on for people watching.

The smallest kid in our class won it, and he crossed the line looking more astonished than pleased. Bess clapped harder than the rest of us put together, and kept clapping after everybody else had stopped.
qs: Why does Bess never make anything of winning?
The author says that is what makes it bearable for the rest of them.
Why did Bess tell nobody about her leg?
Telling somebody would have meant not running.
What detail shows Bess was genuinely pleased for the winner?
She kept clapping after everybody else had stopped.

write.task: Is it more important to win or to be a good sport? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Misplaced Postcard
paras: Gran sent me a postcard from the sea. It never came.
She was upset. She had written it on the first day and posted it the same morning.
Three weeks later it turned up. It had been misplaced in the sorting room.
The postmark was blurred and one corner was bent, but I could read every word.
I have it on my wall now. It was worth the wait.
qs: Who sent the postcard?
Gran sent it from the sea.
Why was the postcard late?
It had been misplaced in the sorting room.
What was wrong with the postcard when it came?
The postmark was blurred and one corner was bent.

write.task: Tell what happened to the postcard, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Misplaced Postcard
paras: Gran sent me a postcard on the first morning of her holiday, and for three weeks it simply did not arrive.
She was more upset about it than I was. She had written it sitting on the harbour wall before breakfast and posted it the same hour.
It turned up eventually, long after she had come home herself. Somewhere in the sorting office it had been misplaced, and nobody could say for how long or where.
The postmark had smudged, one corner was bent right over, and there was a mark across the back that might have been tea. Every word was still readable.
It is on my bedroom wall now, bent corner and all. I would not swap it for one that had arrived on time.
qs: When did Gran write the postcard?
On the first morning, sitting on the harbour wall before breakfast.
Where had the postcard been?
Misplaced somewhere in the sorting office.
Why does the narrator keep the damaged postcard?
They would not swap it for one that arrived on time.

write.task: Explain how a letter gets from one person to another. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Misplaced Postcard
paras: Gran sent me a postcard on the first morning of her holiday, and then, for three entire weeks, nothing whatsoever arrived.

She was considerably more upset about this than I was. She had written it sitting on the harbour wall before breakfast, walked it to the postbox herself within the hour, and told me that night that it was already on its way.

It turned up eventually, a fortnight after she had come home. Somewhere inside the sorting office it had been misplaced, and the post office could not say where it had been, how long it had been there, or how it had got out again.

The postmark had smudged into something unreadable. One corner was bent right over and had stayed bent. There was a brown mark across the back of it that might have been tea and might have been anything. Every single word was still perfectly readable.

It has been on my bedroom wall ever since, bent corner and all. I would not swap it for an identical one that had turned up on time, and I have thought about why, and I think it is because this one had to get here.
qs: What three things could the post office not say?
Where it had been, how long, or how it got out again.
What two things might the brown mark have been?
Tea, or anything.
Why does the narrator value this postcard more?
Because this one had to get here, having been lost and found.

write.task: Write about something that arrived late or was lost and found. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use sensory details.

g2.title: Hopping to the Finish
paras: Our school had a hopping race on sports day.
You had to hop the whole way on one leg. Stopping meant starting again.
Robbie was winning. Then he got the giggles and fell sideways in the grass.
He got up and kept hopping. He was grinning the whole time.
He came last, and he was the only one still hopping at the end.
qs: What was the rule of the race?
You had to hop the whole way on one leg, and stopping meant starting again.
Why did Robbie fall?
He got the giggles and fell sideways in the grass.
Why is coming last not the whole story?
He was the only one still hopping at the end.

write.task: Tell what happened in the race, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: Hopping to the Finish
paras: Our school holds a hopping race every sports day, and nobody can remember who started it or why.
The rules are simple and strictly enforced. One leg, the whole way, and if you put the other foot down you go back and begin again.
Robbie was winning it comfortably until about halfway, when he got the giggles and went over sideways into the grass at some speed.
He got up, went back to the start as the rules demand, and began hopping again, grinning the entire time.
He finished last by a long way. He was also the only person on that field still hopping when he crossed the line.
qs: How long has the race been going?
Nobody can remember who started it or why.
What happens if you put the other foot down?
You go back and begin again.
How did Robbie finish?
Last by a long way, but still hopping.

write.task: Should Robbie have gone back to the start? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: Hopping to the Finish
paras: Our school holds a hopping race on sports day every June. Nobody can remember who began the tradition, why anybody thought it was a good idea, or when it became the event that everybody actually turns up to watch.

The rules are short and they are enforced without mercy by whichever teacher is holding the whistle. One leg. The whole distance. If the other foot touches the ground at any point you return to the start line and begin again from nothing.

Robbie was winning it comfortably, perhaps fifteen metres clear, when at about the halfway mark he caught somebody's eye in the crowd and got the giggles, and went over sideways into the grass at a speed that made several parents stand up.

He picked himself up. He walked all the way back to the start line, because those are the rules and he was not going to be the person who ignored them, and then he set off again, grinning, with the entire field already far ahead of him.

He finished last by a considerable distance. He was also the only competitor on that field still hopping when he crossed the line, and the noise when he did was louder than it had been for the winner.
qs: What does the author say the race has become?
The event that everybody actually turns up to watch.
Why did Robbie walk back to the start?
Those are the rules and he would not be the person who ignored them.
What does the noise at the end tell you?
The crowd admired finishing honestly more than winning.

write.task: Should rules always be followed exactly? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Giant of the Village
paras: In the centre of our village there is a huge stone giant.
The story says he was kind. He carried the stones for the arch on his own.
The city sent men to help, but by the time they came the arch was finished.
Once a year we place a ring of lamps round the giant.
My gran says the giant is a nice story. I think a nice story can still be real.
qs: Where is the stone giant?
In the centre of our village.
What did the giant do?
He carried the stones for the arch on his own.
What do the villagers do once a year?
They place a ring of lamps round the giant.

write.task: Is the story of the giant true? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Giant of the Village
paras: In the centre of our village there is a stone figure of a giant, twice as tall as a person, facing the bridge.
The story goes that he was gentle, and that he carried every stone for that bridge down from the ridge himself, one at a time, over a single winter.
The city sent a gang of men to help with the work. By the time they arrived the bridge was finished and the giant had gone.
Once a year the village places a circle of candles around the base of the stone figure and leaves them to burn down.
My gran says it is a nice story and nothing more. I have never been able to see why a nice story cannot also be a real one.
qs: How tall is the stone figure?
Twice as tall as a person.
What happened when the city's men arrived?
The bridge was finished and the giant had gone.
What does Gran think of the story?
That it is a nice story and nothing more.

write.task: Write the winter the giant built the bridge. Use time-order words and describe what the work was like.

g4.title: The Giant of the Village
paras: In the centre of our village, facing the bridge, there is a stone stone figure of a giant. It stands twice the height of a grown person and it has been there longer than any record the parish council can produce.

The story, which everybody here is told before they are six, is that he was gentle. That he carried every single stone for that bridge down from the ridge himself, one at a time, across the course of one winter, and that he did it because the village needed a crossing and nobody else was going to build one.

The city, when it finally noticed, sent a gang of men up with carts and ropes to assist. By the time they arrived at the top of the valley the bridge was standing, the last stone was in place, and the giant was nowhere to be found.
Once a year, on the first Sunday in December, the village sets a circle of candles around the base of the stone figure and lets them burn right down. Nobody has ever decided this. It simply happens.
My gran says it is a nice story and that is all it is. I have never once been able to work out why a nice story should not also be a true one, and I have decided not to ask her again.
qs: Why does the story say the giant built the bridge?
The village needed a crossing and nobody else was going to build one.
What is unusual about the December candles?
Nobody has ever decided it — it simply happens.
Why has the narrator decided not to ask Gran again?
Because they disagree and do not want the argument.

write.task: Write a report on a local story or landmark. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Badger at the Edge
paras: There is a badger that lives at the edge of our garden, under the hedge.
We never see it. We only see the ridge of earth it pushes up each night.
Dad put a camera by the bridge over the ditch to catch it.
For six nights there was nothing. On the seventh the badger walked straight past the lens.
We have the picture on the fridge now. It is not a good picture. We do not care.
qs: Where does the badger live?
At the edge of our garden, under the hedge.
What did Dad do to catch it?
He put a camera by the bridge over the ditch.
How many nights was there nothing?
Six nights.

write.task: Write three facts about the badger from the story. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Badger at the Edge
paras: There is a badger living at the edge of our garden, somewhere under the hedge where the ground drops away towards the ditch.
We have never once seen it. All we ever see is the fresh ridge of earth it pushes up overnight, in a slightly different place each morning.
In August Dad set up a camera on a post beside the little bridge over the ditch, pointed at the gap in the hedge, and left it there.
For six nights it recorded absolutely nothing except a very bored-looking fox. On the seventh the badger walked straight past the lens without glancing at it.
The picture is on the fridge now. It is blurred, it is off-centre, and most of the badger is out of frame. Nobody in this house cares in the slightest.
qs: What is the only sign of the badger?
The fresh ridge of earth it pushes up overnight.
What did the camera record for six nights?
Nothing except a very bored-looking fox.
What is wrong with the picture?
It is blurred, off-centre, and most of the badger is out of frame.

write.task: Write the seventh night from the badger's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could smell and hear.

g4.title: The Badger at the Edge
paras: There is a badger living at the edge of our garden, somewhere beneath the hedge at the point where the ground gives up and drops away towards the ditch. We have known about it for three years.

In all that time we have never once seen it. What we see is the evidence: a fresh ridge of turned earth pushed up overnight, in a slightly different place every morning, as though it were working its way along the hedge to a plan it has not shared with us.
In August Dad fixed a camera to a post beside the small bridge over the ditch, aimed it squarely at the gap in the hedge where the ridge usually appeared, and left it out there for a week.

For six consecutive nights it recorded nothing whatsoever except a fox, which came past at approximately the same time each night and looked, in every single frame, profoundly unimpressed by the whole arrangement.

On the seventh night the badger walked straight past the lens without so much as turning its head. The picture is on the fridge now. It is blurred, it is badly off-centre, and a good third of the animal is outside the frame entirely. Nobody in this house cares even slightly.
qs: How long have they known about the badger?
Three years.
What does the author suggest about the badger's plan?
That it is working along the hedge to a plan it has not shared.
How did the fox appear in every frame?
Profoundly unimpressed by the whole arrangement.

write.task: Is it better to watch wildlife with a camera or with your own eyes? Group your reasons, support them with details, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Robot in the Basement
paras: Our friend Sam built a robot in his basement. He began it in April.
It has a motor, a silver body, and a tiny radio inside its head.
It cannot walk. It can only spin slowly on the spot and hum.
I think it is the finest thing I have ever seen. Sam is not so sure.
He says a robot that only spins is a lamp. I say it is a robot that likes to dance.
qs: Where did Sam build the robot?
In his basement.
What is inside the robot's head?
A tiny radio.
What does Sam say the robot really is?
He says a robot that only spins is a lamp.

write.task: Is the robot a real robot? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Robot in the Basement
paras: My uncle began house a robot in his basement in April, and by the middle of August it was finished, or finished enough to look at.
It stands about the size of a chair. It has a motor, a silver body made from a bin lid, and a tiny radio bolted inside its head.
It cannot walk. It has never been able to walk and my uncle has stopped pretending it will. What it can do is rotate slowly on the spot and hum.
I think it is the finest object I have ever been shown. My uncle is a great deal less certain and keeps apologising for it.
He says that a robot which only spins is really just a lamp. I say that it is a robot that happens to like dancing, and so far not one of us has given way.
qs: How long did the robot take to build?
From April to the middle of August.
What is the silver body made from?
A bin lid.
What is the disagreement about?
Whether a robot that only spins is really a lamp or a robot that likes dancing.

write.task: Explain how to build something simple from things you already have. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Robot in the Basement
paras: My uncle began house a robot in his basement in April. By the middle of August it was finished, or at least finished to the point where he would let people come down and look at it, which is not quite the same thing.

It stands about the size of a kitchen chair. It has a motor he took out of a broken fan, a silver body hammered out of a bin lid, and a tiny radio bolted inside the head so that it makes a faint crackling noise even when it is switched off.

It cannot walk. It has never been able to walk, and some time in June my uncle stopped pretending that it was going to. What it can do, and does, is rotate very slowly on the spot while humming, which it will keep up for as long as you leave it plugged in.

I think it is the finest object anybody has ever shown me. My uncle is a great deal less certain, and he has apologised for it every single time I have been down there, which cannot be good for a person.

He maintains that a robot which only spins is, in honest terms, a lamp. I maintain that it is a robot that happens to enjoy dancing. Not one of us has moved an inch on this in four months and I do not expect that to change.
qs: Where did the motor come from?
A broken fan.
Why does the robot crackle when switched off?
There is a tiny radio bolted inside its head.
What does the author imply about the uncle apologising?
That it cannot be good for him to keep running down his own work.

write.task: Write about making something that did not turn out as planned. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: The Noise in the Attic
paras: There was a noise in the attic all the fall. A scratching, and then a pause.
Mum said it was the house settling. Dad said it was a bird.
I thought it was something else. I had heard a small voice up there.
In October we found them: four kittens in a box of straw, and a thin grey cat guarding the lot.
They live in the kitchen now. Nobody mentions the house settling any more.
qs: How long was there a noise in the attic?
All the fall.
What did Mum and Dad each think it was?
Mum said the house settling and Dad said a bird.
What was really up there?
Four kittens in a box of straw and a thin grey cat.

write.task: Tell how the kittens were found, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Noise in the Attic
paras: There was a noise in the attic for most of that the fall. A scratching sound, then a long pause, then the scratching again.
Mum was certain it was the house settling, which is the answer she gives to every sound a house makes. Dad was equally certain it was a bird that had got in under the slates.
I thought they were both avoiding the obvious. Twice, late on, I had heard something that was unmistakably a small voice.
We went up with a torch on the first Saturday in October and found four kittens in a box of straw behind the water tank, with a thin grey cat sitting in front of them refusing to move.
All five of them live in the kitchen now. Nobody in this house has mentioned the house settling since.
qs: What answer does Mum give to every house noise?
That the house is settling.
What had the narrator heard twice?
Something that was unmistakably a small voice.
What was the grey cat doing?
Sitting in front of the kittens refusing to move.

write.task: Should the family have kept the cats? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Noise in the Attic
paras: There was a noise in the attic for most of that the fall. It went in a pattern you could set a clock by: a scratching, for perhaps half a minute, then a long and deliberate pause, then the scratching again.

Mum was entirely certain it was the house settling. This is the answer she gives to every sound a house has ever made, and she gives it with such confidence that people generally stop asking. Dad was equally certain, and equally untroubled, that it was a bird that had got in under the slates.

I thought they were both quietly avoiding the obvious. Twice, late in the evening, with the television off, I had heard something from up there that was not a bird and was not a joist. It was unmistakably a small voice.

We went up with a torch on the first Saturday in October. Behind the water tank, in a cardboard box somebody had filled with straw years before, there were four kittens. In front of them, between them and us, sat a thin grey cat who had no intention of moving for anybody.
All five of them live in the kitchen now, on a blanket by the boiler, and nobody in this house has mentioned the house settling at any point since.
qs: How does the author describe the pattern of the noise?
Scratching for half a minute, a long deliberate pause, then scratching again.
Why do people stop asking Mum about house noises?
She answers with such confidence that they stop asking.
What two things did the narrator rule out?
A bird and a joist.

write.task: Write a report on how to care for a cat and her kittens. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: Making the Model
paras: Our class is making a model of the village out of card.
I am sticking the roofs on. Tam is shaping the trees.
We kept losing the small pieces, so we began using a lid to hold them.
By Friday the whole thing is standing, and it is hiding nothing. Every house is there.
We are taking it to the hall on Monday so the school can see it.
qs: What is the class making?
A model of the village out of card.
How did they stop losing the small pieces?
They began using a lid to hold them.
Where is the model going on Monday?
To the hall, so the school can see it.

write.task: Write three facts about making the model. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: Making the Model
paras: Our class spent three weeks making a model of the village out of card, and it very nearly did not get finished.
I was sticking roofs on. Tam was shaping trees out of wire and green paper, which turned out to be the slowest job in the room by a long way.
We kept losing the small pieces into the carpet, until somebody had the sense to start using a tin lid as a tray. After that we lost nothing.
By Friday afternoon the whole village was standing on two tables pushed together, and it was hiding nothing. Every single house on our road was on it, including the empty one.
We are carrying it down to the hall on Monday, very slowly, so the rest of the school can have a look.
qs: How long did the model take?
Three weeks.
What was the slowest job?
Shaping trees out of wire and green paper.
How do you know the model was complete?
Every house on the road was on it, including the empty one.

write.task: Write about a project you worked on with other people. Use time-order words and include dialogue.

g4.title: Making the Model
paras: Our class spent three weeks making a model of the village out of card, and there was a stretch in the middle of the second week when it very nearly did not get finished at all.

I was sticking roofs on, which is straightforward and which I would recommend. Tam was shaping trees out of wire and green tissue paper, one at a time, and that turned out to be the slowest job in the room by a distance nobody had anticipated.

The real problem was losing things. Small pieces went into the carpet at a rate of about one every ten minutes and were never seen again, until somebody finally had the sense to start using a tin lid as a holding tray. After that we did not lose a single thing.

By Friday afternoon the entire village was standing on two tables pushed end to end, and it was hiding nothing. Every house on our road was on it, in order, including the empty one at the far end that nobody ever mentions.
We are carrying it down to the hall on Monday morning, very slowly indeed and with four people on the corners, so that the rest of the school can come and have a look at it.
qs: At what rate were pieces being lost?
About one every ten minutes.
What detail shows the model was honest about the village?
It included the empty house at the far end that nobody mentions.
Why will four people carry it?
So it is not dropped or damaged on the way to the hall.

write.task: Is group work better than working alone? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Happiest Day
paras: Last summer was the hottest we have had, and the days were the longest too.
We carried water to the garden every evening and studied the sky for rain.
None came. The grass dried and the leaves curled and nothing in the beds got any taller.
Then one Friday the sky went grey and it rained for an hour.
We stood out in it and got soaked, and it was the happiest I have been in a garden.
qs: What was last summer like?
It was the hottest they have had and the days were the longest.
What did they do every evening?
They carried water to the garden and studied the sky for rain.
Why were they so happy on Friday?
Because it finally rained for an hour.

write.task: Tell what happened in the garden, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: The Happiest Day
paras: Last summer was the hottest anybody round here can remember, and the days seemed to go on much longer than days normally do.
We carried water out to the garden every single evening and studied the sky afterwards, hoping. My little sister took it the most seriously of any of us.
Nothing came. The grass dried out to straw, the leaves on the bean plants curled up at the edges, and for six weeks almost nothing in those beds got any taller.
Then on a Friday in August the sky went grey in about ten minutes and it rained properly for a whole hour.
We went out and stood in it and got completely soaked, all four of us, and it remains the happiest I have ever been in a garden.
qs: How long did almost nothing get taller?
Six weeks.
Who took the watering most seriously?
The narrator's little sister.
How quickly did the sky change?
In about ten minutes.

write.task: Explain how to keep a garden alive in dry weather. Group your steps and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Happiest Day
paras: Last summer was the hottest anybody round here can remember, and the days seemed to stretch out considerably longer than days have any business stretching.

We carried water out to the garden every single evening, two cans each, and then stood about studying the sky afterwards as though looking hard enough might help. My younger sister took this part more seriously than the rest of us put together and kept a chart.

Nothing came. The grass dried out to straw and went crisp underfoot. The leaves on the bean plants curled up at the edges and then browned. For six solid weeks almost nothing in that garden grew by any amount worth measuring.
Then on a Friday afternoon in the middle of August the sky went from blue to grey in about ten minutes, with no warning any of us had noticed, and it rained properly and heavily for a full hour.

We went out and stood in it. All four of us, in the middle of the lawn, getting steadily and completely soaked and not one of us suggesting we go back in. It remains, without any competition, the happiest I have ever been in a garden.
qs: What did the younger sister keep?
A chart.
What two stages did the bean leaves go through?
They curled at the edges and then browned.
Why does the author mention nobody suggested going in?
To show how much they were all enjoying the rain.

write.task: Is it worth keeping a garden? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.

g2.title: The Robin and the Shed
paras: A robin built a nest on the shelf in our shed in April.
We could not finish the painting. We could not even open the door properly.
Dad put a wedge under it so the gap stayed the same all month.
The robin did not seem to mind us at all. It came and went past our heads.
By June the young had gone. We finished the shed in one afternoon.
qs: Where did the robin build its nest?
On the shelf in the shed.
Why could they not open the door properly?
Because the robin had a nest inside and they kept the gap the same.
When did they finish the shed?
In June, after the young had gone.

write.task: Was it right to stop work for the robin? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Robin and the Shed
paras: A robin built its nest on the top shelf of our shed in the first week of April, which was awkward, because the shed was half painted.
We stopped. You cannot finish a shed with a robin in it, and anyway opening the door more than a hand's width made the bird panic.
Dad put a wooden wedge under the door so that the gap stayed exactly the same for the whole of April and May, and we went in sideways when we had to.
After the first fortnight the robin stopped minding us entirely. It would come and go past our heads with food in its beak as though we were part of the furniture.
By the second week of June the young had all gone. We finished the painting in a single afternoon and left the wedge where it was, in case.
qs: Why was the nest awkward?
The shed was half painted and the work had to stop.
What did the wedge do?
It kept the door gap exactly the same for April and May.
Why did they leave the wedge in place?
In case the robin comes back.

write.task: Write the two months from the robin's point of view. Use time-order words and describe what it could see and hear.

g4.title: The Robin and the Shed
paras: A robin built its nest on the top shelf of our shed in the first week of April. This was awkward, because the shed was at that point half painted, with one wall done, one wall undercoated and a tin of green gloss open on the floor.

We stopped. There is no sensible way to finish a shed with a robin living in it, and in any case we established within about a day that opening the door more than a hand's width sent the bird into a panic that was unpleasant to watch.

So Dad cut a wooden wedge and put it under the door, and for the whole of April and the whole of May that gap did not change by so much as a finger's width. Anybody who needed anything out of that shed went in sideways and came out the same way.

After the first fortnight the robin stopped minding us altogether. It would come and go directly past our heads with food in its beak, at speed, as though we were a particularly dull piece of garden furniture it had long ago stopped noticing.
By the second week of June the young had all gone, and the shelf was empty. We finished the painting in a single afternoon. The wedge is still under the door, and nobody has suggested moving it.
qs: What state was the shed in when the robin arrived?
One wall done, one undercoated, and a tin of green gloss open on the floor.
What did they learn within a day?
That opening the door more than a hand's width panicked the bird.
What does leaving the wedge show?
They hope the robin will come back next year.

write.task: Write a report on how birds build and use nests. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: The Wobbly Table
paras: The table in our kitchen is terrible. One leg is shorter than the other three.
It wobbles whenever anybody puts an elbow on it. Every bottle falls over.
Gran folded a little piece of cardboard and pushed it under the short leg.
The wobble stopped at once. It was that simple.
Dad had been planning to buy a new table for a year. He is a bit annoyed.
qs: What is wrong with the table?
One leg is shorter than the other three, so it wobbles.
What did Gran do?
She folded a little piece of cardboard and pushed it under the short leg.
Why is Dad annoyed?
He had been planning to buy a new table for a year.

write.task: Write three facts about fixing the table. Start with a topic sentence and finish with an ending.

g3.title: The Wobbly Table
paras: The table in our kitchen is terrible and has been terrible for as long as I have been able to reach it. One leg is a little shorter than the other three.
It wobbles whenever anybody rests an elbow on it, which is constantly, and every bottle that has ever been set near the middle has eventually gone over.
Gran came for lunch in September, watched this happen twice, and then folded a piece of cardboard into four and pushed it under the short leg without comment.
The wobble stopped immediately and has not come back once. The whole repair took her about nine seconds and cost nothing at all.
Dad had been planning to buy a replacement table for the better part of a year. He has not said much about it since.
qs: How long has the table been terrible?
As long as the narrator has been able to reach it.
What did Gran do before fixing it?
She watched a bottle go over twice.
How long did the repair take?
About nine seconds.

write.task: Is it better to mend things or replace them? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: The Wobbly Table
paras: The table in our kitchen is terrible, and it has been terrible for as long as I have been tall enough to reach the top of it. One leg is fractionally shorter than the other three. Not visibly. Just enough.

It wobbles whenever anybody rests an elbow on it, which in this house is more or less continuously, and every bottle that has ever been set down near the middle of it has, given sufficient time, gone over.

Gran came for lunch in September. She watched a bottle of squash go over twice in twenty minutes without saying anything about it. Then she got up, folded a piece of cardboard into four, crouched down, and pushed it under the short leg.

The wobble stopped immediately. It has not come back, not once, in the seven months since. The entire repair took her about nine seconds and cost precisely nothing, and she went back to her lunch without mentioning it again.
Dad had been planning to replace that table for the better part of a year. He had looked at three in a shop in town. He has not said a great deal about any of it since September.
qs: How short is the leg?
Fractionally — not visibly, just enough.
How did Gran behave before fixing it?
She watched it happen twice without saying anything.
What had Dad already done about the table?
He had looked at three replacements in a shop in town.

write.task: Write about a problem somebody solved in a surprisingly simple way. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue.

g2.title: A Banana for the Walk
paras: We were about to set off on a long walk along the canal.
Mum gave us each a banana and a bottle of water to carry.
Ahead of us the path went away into the trees and we could not see the end of it.
An hour along, my brother sat down on a wall and ate his banana in about four bites.
Mine lasted the whole way. I am aware that this was the only part of the walk I won.
qs: Where were they walking?
Along the canal.
What did Mum give them?
A banana and a bottle of water each.
How fast did the brother eat his banana?
In about four bites.

write.task: Tell what happened on the walk, in order. Use first, next, and last.

g3.title: A Banana for the Walk
paras: We were about to set off on a long walk along the canal, the sort that is announced as an hour and turns out to be three.
Mum handed us each a banana and a bottle of water at the gate and told us to carry our own, which was fair.
Ahead of us the towpath ran away into the trees and simply kept going. You could not see the end of it from the start, which is the whole trouble with canals.
About an hour along, my brother sat down on a low wall and ate his banana in about four bites, then spent the remaining two hours mentioning that he was hungry.
Mine lasted the entire way. I am well aware that this was the only part of that walk I won, and I have never let him forget it.
qs: How long was the walk announced as?
An hour, but it turned out to be three.
What is 'the whole trouble with canals'?
You cannot see the end of the path from the start.
What did the brother do for the last two hours?
He kept mentioning that he was hungry.

write.task: Is it better to save a treat or eat it straight away? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: A Banana for the Walk
paras: We were about to set off on a long walk along the canal. It had been announced to us as an hour. It was, in the end, a little over three, which is the usual arrangement with walks in our family and by now it surprises nobody.
Mum handed us each a banana and a bottle of water at the gate and told us we were carrying our own, which was perfectly fair and which both of us immediately complained about anyway.

Ahead of us the towpath ran away into the trees and then simply kept going. You cannot see the end of a canal from the beginning of it. That is the entire trouble with canals, and it is why the first hour always feels like the whole walk.

About an hour along, my brother sat himself down on a low wall and ate his banana in approximately four bites, with every appearance of satisfaction, and then spent the remaining two hours of the afternoon mentioning at regular intervals that he was hungry.
Mine lasted the entire distance, in small pieces, all the way to the last bridge. I am aware that this was the only part of that walk I won, and I have never once allowed him to forget about it.
qs: What is the 'usual arrangement' with walks in this family?
They are announced as much shorter than they turn out to be.
Why does the first hour feel like the whole walk?
Because you cannot see the end of a canal from the beginning.
How did the narrator make the banana last?
By eating it in small pieces all the way to the last bridge.

write.task: Write a report on how to prepare for a long walk. Organise it into sections, develop each with facts and examples, and connect your ideas.

g2.title: She Won't Say Why
paras: My sister won't tell me where she goes on Saturday mornings.
She isn't rude about it. She just says, “You'll find out,” and gets her coat.
I don't like not knowing. I've tried asking Mum, who won't say.
Last week I followed her. She's been helping at the animal shelter since March.
She didn't mind me knowing. She said, “I'd have told you. You'd have wanted to come.”
qs: What won't the sister say?
Where she goes on Saturday mornings.
Where does she actually go?
She has been helping at the animal shelter since March.
Why didn't she tell anybody?
She says the narrator would have wanted to come.

write.task: Tell what happened on Saturday, in order. Use first, next, and last, and include something somebody said.

g3.title: She Won't Say Why
paras: My sister won't tell anybody where she goes on Saturday mornings, and she's been going since the start of the year.
She isn't rude about it, which somehow makes it worse. She just says, “You'll find out eventually,” picks up her coat, and leaves before anybody can argue.
I don't like not knowing things. I'd asked Mum twice, and Mum, who clearly does know, wouldn't say a word.
So last Saturday I followed her at a distance all the way into town, and she went straight into the animal shelter on Mill Street and put on an apron.
She didn't mind being caught. She said, “I'd have told you months ago. You'd have wanted to come, and they don't take anybody under twelve.”
qs: How long has the sister been going?
Since the start of the year.
What makes it worse that she isn't rude?
It leaves the narrator with nothing to argue about.
Why hadn't she said anything?
The narrator would have wanted to come and they don't take anybody under twelve.

write.task: Was the sister right to keep it secret? Give your opinion with reasons, using because and also to link them.

g4.title: She Won't Say Why
paras: My sister won't tell anybody in this house where she goes on Saturday mornings. She's been going since the first week of January, she leaves at ten past eight, and she's back by one, and that is the entire sum of what we know.

She isn't rude about it, which somehow makes the whole thing worse. If she snapped at us we'd have something to be annoyed about. Instead she says, “You'll find out eventually,” in a perfectly pleasant voice, picks up her coat, and is out of the door before anybody has assembled a follow-up question.

I don't like not knowing things. I'd asked Mum about it twice. Mum knows — that much is obvious from her face every time the subject comes up — and Mum wouldn't say a single word either, which I thought was unfair of both of them.

So last Saturday I followed her. All the way down the hill, through town, past the market, and in through the side door of the animal shelter on Mill Street, where she took an apron off a hook and put it on like somebody who'd done it a hundred times.

She didn't mind being caught, in the end. She said, “I'd have told you months ago. But you'd have wanted to come, and they won't take anybody under twelve, and I didn't fancy having that argument every week until your birthday.”
qs: What exactly does the family know?
That she leaves at ten past eight and is back by one.
Why would it be easier if she snapped at them?
Then they would have something to be annoyed about.
What argument was the sister avoiding?
Having to refuse to take the narrator every week until their birthday.

write.task: Write the Saturday from the sister's point of view. Establish the situation, give a clear sequence, and use dialogue and sensory details.

g2.title: The Station Question
paras: Our station is tiny. One platform, one bench, and a sign with no information on it.
The six o'clock train had not come. There was no explanation and nobody to ask.
A man in a grey coat said it was cancelled. He gave no reason for that opinion.
Then the station master came out and said there was a problem with a signal.
The train came at seven. The man in the grey coat said he had known all along.
qs: What is on the platform?
One bench and a sign with no information on it.
What did the station master say?
That there was a problem with a signal.
What did the man in the grey coat claim at the end?
That he had known all along.

write.task: Should the man have said the train was cancelled? Tell what you think, give two reasons, and write an ending.

g3.title: The Station Question
paras: Our station is tiny. One platform, one bench, one sign that has never in living memory carried any information at all.
On Thursday the six o'clock train did not arrive. There was no announcement, no explanation on the board, and nobody on the platform in any kind of uniform.
A man in a grey coat announced to everybody that it had been cancelled. He offered no reason for this opinion and nobody asked him for one, which is how these things go.
Twenty minutes later the station master came out of the office and told us there was a fault on a signal two stations up the line and the train was running late.
It arrived at seven. The man in the grey coat told the carriage he had known about the signal all along.
qs: What has the sign never carried?
Any information at all.
What was the real reason for the delay?
A fault on a signal two stations up the line.
Why is the man's final claim hard to believe?
He had offered no reason earlier and had said it was cancelled.

write.task: Explain how information should be given to people who are waiting. Group your points and use words like first, then, and finally.

g4.title: The Station Question
paras: Our station is tiny. One platform, one bench, and a single electronic sign which has not, in the memory of anybody currently alive, displayed any information whatsoever about any train.

On Tuesday evening the six o'clock did not arrive. There was no announcement over the speakers, no explanation on the board, and not one member of staff visible anywhere on the platform or in the ticket office behind it.

After about four minutes of this a man in a grey coat announced to the platform in general that the train had been cancelled. He offered no evidence for this position and nobody present asked him for any, which is, in my experience, exactly how these situations develop.

Twenty minutes later the station master came out of the office with a radio in his hand and told us there was a fault on a signal two stations up the line, that the train was held there, and that it would be with us inside the hour.
It arrived at seven minutes past. As we got on, the man in the grey coat was explaining to the whole carriage that he had known about the signal from the beginning.
qs: How long after six did the man speak?
About four minutes.
What did the station master have in his hand?
A radio.
What does the author imply about claims made with no evidence?
That people accept them without asking, which is how such situations develop.

write.task: Should people speak up when they do not actually know? Group your reasons, support them with details from the text, and end with a conclusion.
